nodes.title: Counting and Numbers 1–9
nodes.description: Counting tells us how many things there are. We say one number name for each object, and the last number we say tells the size of the whole group. This idea — that numbers stand for 'how many' — is the foundation of all arithmetic.
learning_outcomes: Can count up to 9 objects, touching each object exactly once
Can say how many objects there are after counting, without recounting
Can recognise and write the numerals 1 to 9
Can count out a requested number of objects from a larger pile

misconceptions.description: Counting is just reciting a rhyme; the last number said is not understood as the size of the whole group (missing cardinality).
misconceptions.signal: After counting 5 toys aloud, when asked 'so how many toys?', the child recounts from 1 or repeats the whole sequence instead of answering '5'.
misconceptions.remedy: After each count, cover the objects and ask 'how many are hiding?'. Emphasise the last-word rule with tiny sets (2-3 objects) where the child can see the answer instantly.

misconceptions.description: Rearranging objects changes how many there are (no conservation of number).
misconceptions.signal: Counts 7 shells, watches them being spread out, and expects a different answer or insists on recounting because the row 'got bigger'.
misconceptions.remedy: Count together, rearrange while the child watches, and ask 'did any shell come or go?'. Repeat with clumping, stacking and spreading until the child predicts 'still 7' confidently.

misconceptions.description: One-to-one correspondence is unstable: objects get skipped or counted twice.
misconceptions.signal: Says number names faster or slower than the finger points; the same pile gives a different count each attempt.
misconceptions.remedy: Use touch-and-move counting: physically slide each counted object into a 'done' pile so nothing can be skipped or recounted.

real_world_hooks: Counting rotis on a plate at dinner
Counting steps while climbing stairs
Counting bangles on Amma's wrist
Counting spoons while setting the table
teaching.video_search: counting objects 1 to 9 for kids one to one correspondence

questions.prompt: Count the mangoes: 🥭 🥭 🥭 🥭 🥭. How many mangoes are there?

options.diagnosis: Skipped one mango while counting.
Counted one mango twice.
Recited the number rhyme to the end instead of stopping at the last object.

questions.explanation: Touch each mango once as you count: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The last number you say, 5, tells how many mangoes there are in all.

questions.prompt: You counted 7 shells in a line. Then you spread the shells far apart, so the line looks much longer. How many shells are there now?

options.diagnosis: Thinks moving objects can change the count.

options.text: You cannot tell without counting again

questions.explanation: No shell was added and no shell was taken away, so there are still 7 shells. Spreading things out changes how the group LOOKS, not how many there ARE.

questions.prompt: Raju counted his toy cars: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. What does the number 7 tell us?

options.text: Only the last car is called 7
7 is just the name of one car
He must count again to be sure
options.diagnosis: Does not trust a careful one-to-one count.

questions.explanation: When we count, the last number we say tells us how many things there are altogether. So 7 means the whole group has 7 cars — not just the last one.

nodes.title: Zero and Its Meaning
nodes.description: Zero is the number that tells us there is nothing to count. It is a real number with its own symbol, 0, and its own place on the number line just before 1. Understanding zero prepares us for place value and for adding and subtracting.
learning_outcomes: Can say that zero means 'none' and write the numeral 0
Can place 0 correctly before 1 when ordering numbers
Can answer 'how many' questions where the answer is zero
Can add and take away zero from a small number correctly

misconceptions.description: Zero means 'nothing', so it is not a real number and cannot be an answer.
misconceptions.signal: When a plate is empty, says 'there is no number for it' or refuses to write 0 as an answer.
misconceptions.remedy: Play games where groups shrink to empty: 'How many biscuits now? 3... 2... 1... 0!' Write 0 each time so the child sees zero used as a genuine answer.

misconceptions.description: Zero's position in the number order is unknown — it is placed after 9 (like on a phone keypad) or left off the number line entirely.
misconceptions.signal: Orders numbers as 1, 2, ..., 9, 0, or cannot say what comes before 1 when counting down.
misconceptions.remedy: Do rocket-countdown chants (3, 2, 1, 0, blast off!) and walk a floor number line starting at 0, so zero's home just before 1 becomes physical.

misconceptions.description: Adding zero destroys the number: n + 0 = 0, because 'zero means nothing is left'.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 5 + 0 = 0, explaining 'you added nothing so there is nothing'.
misconceptions.remedy: Act it out: put 5 biscuits on one plate and 0 on another, push the plates together and count. Adding an empty plate changes nothing — the 5 biscuits are all still there.

real_world_hooks: An empty tiffin box after lunch
Rocket countdown 3-2-1-0
Zero runs scored off a ball in cricket (a dot ball)
An empty bird's nest after the birds fly away
teaching.video_search: concept of zero for grade 1 kids empty set counting down

questions.prompt: A plate had 3 laddoos. You ate all 3. How many laddoos are on the plate now?

options.diagnosis: Answered with the starting amount instead of what is left.
Thinks at least one must always remain; did not count the empty plate.

options.text: There is no number for an empty plate

questions.explanation: All 3 laddoos are gone, so the plate has none. The number for 'none' is zero, written 0. Zero is a real number and a perfectly good answer!

questions.prompt: What is 4 + 0?

options.diagnosis: Treated the 0 as if it were 1 and counted on.
Wrote the two digits side by side instead of adding.

questions.explanation: Adding 0 means adding nothing at all. You had 4, you added nothing, so you still have 4. Adding zero never changes a number.

questions.prompt: A rocket countdown goes: 3, 2, 1, ___. What comes next, just before blast off?

options.diagnosis: Counted up instead of down.
Placed zero after the other numbers, like on a phone keypad.

questions.explanation: Counting down goes 3, 2, 1, 0. Zero sits just before 1 — it is the number that means 'none left'. Blast off!

nodes.title: Numbers up to 20
nodes.description: The numbers 10 to 20 are our first step beyond one hand and one foot of counting! Each 'teen' number is really a ten and some more — 14 is 10 and 4. Seeing this hidden ten is the first big idea of place value.
learning_outcomes: Can count objects up to 20 accurately
Can read and write numerals 10 to 20 and say them in order
Can show a teen number as one group of ten and some ones
Can say which of two numbers up to 20 is more

misconceptions.description: Teen number names and digits get reversed: 'fourteen' is written 41 because the 'four' is heard first.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 41 for fourteen, 51 for fifteen; reads 13 as thirty-one.
misconceptions.remedy: Use place-value cards: lay the 10 card down, slide the 4 on top of the 0, and say 'fourteen is TEN and FOUR'. The ten is written first even though English says the ones first.

misconceptions.description: The teen counting sequence has rote gaps — some numbers are always skipped.
misconceptions.signal: Counts '...thirteen, fourteen, sixteen, seventeen', consistently missing the same number (often fifteen).
misconceptions.remedy: Choral counting with a number chart, pointing to each numeral. Pause dramatically just before the skipped number and let the child supply it, then drill just that bridge.

misconceptions.description: Teen numbers are not seen as 'ten and some more' — every count starts again from 1.
misconceptions.signal: To show 14, counts out 14 loose sticks one by one; cannot answer 'how many tens are in 14?'
misconceptions.remedy: Bundle 10 sticks with a rubber band, then add loose ones: 'ten... eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen'. Use ten-frames so the full frame of 10 is seen at a glance.

real_world_hooks: Bundling 10 pencils with a rubber band at the stationery shop
Egg trays and idli plates that hold groups
Counting all fingers and toes
Ten-rupee note plus loose coins
teaching.video_search: teen numbers ten and some more ten frame grade 1

questions.prompt: Which of these is the number fifteen?

options.diagnosis: Heard only the 'five' part of the word.
Confused 'fifteen' with 'fifty'.

questions.explanation: Fifteen is ten and five. We write the ten part first: 15. Be careful — 51 is fifty-one, a much bigger number!

questions.prompt: What number comes just after 16?

options.diagnosis: Gave the number just BEFORE instead of after.
Skipped a number in the teen sequence.

questions.explanation: Counting on: ...15, 16, 17, 18... So the number just after 16 is 17.

questions.prompt: Meena has one bundle of 10 sticks and 3 loose sticks. How many sticks does she have in all?

options.diagnosis: Counted only the loose sticks; did not include the bundle of ten.
Wrote 10 and 3 side by side instead of combining them into one number.

questions.explanation: The bundle is 10, then count on the loose sticks: 11, 12, 13. Ten and three make thirteen, written 13.

nodes.title: Addition and Subtraction within 20
nodes.description: Adding means putting groups together; subtracting means taking away or finding how many more. With numbers up to 20 we learn smart moves like counting on from the bigger number and making a ten. These small facts become the building blocks for all bigger sums.
learning_outcomes: Can add two numbers with a total up to 20 using objects, fingers or counting on
Can subtract within 20 by taking away or counting back
Can solve simple story problems about joining and taking away
Can find the missing number in facts like 9 + __ = 15

misconceptions.description: When counting on, the starting number itself is counted as the first step (8 + 3: '8, 9, 10' gives 10).
misconceptions.signal: Answers are consistently one less than correct on counting-on problems.
misconceptions.remedy: Say 'put 8 in your head' (tap head), then raise 3 fingers and count ONLY the new ones: '9, 10, 11'. The start number is already done — we count the jumps, not the start.

misconceptions.description: Subtraction works in any order, like addition (subtraction is commutative).
misconceptions.signal: Faced with 4 − 9, calmly answers 5; or reads 12 − 5 but computes 5 from '12 and 5'.
misconceptions.remedy: Act out take-away stories with objects: try to take 9 laddoos from a plate of 4 and discover you can't. Order matters — who starts with the sweets matters!

misconceptions.description: The equals sign means 'the answer comes next', not 'both sides are the same amount'.
misconceptions.signal: Fills 5 + __ = 8 with 13 (adds the two visible numbers); rejects 8 = 3 + 5 as 'written backwards'.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a pan balance or seesaw picture: both sides must weigh the same. Read '=' aloud as 'is the same as', and practise true/false sentences like 7 = 7 and 6 + 1 = 5 + 2.

real_world_hooks: Runs added to a cricket score
Sharing and eating jalebis from a plate
Passengers getting on and off an auto-rickshaw
Marbles won and lost in a game
teaching.video_search: addition subtraction within 20 counting on make a ten grade 1

questions.prompt: What is 7 + 5?

options.diagnosis: Started counting at 7 instead of after it.
Counted one jump too many.
Subtracted instead of adding.

questions.explanation: Put 7 in your head, then count on 5 more: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. Or make a ten: 7 + 3 = 10, then 2 more makes 12.

questions.prompt: What is 14 − 6?

options.diagnosis: Counted back but included the starting number as a step.
Added instead of subtracting.
Answered with the number being taken away.

questions.explanation: Count back 6 from 14: 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 8. Or break it up: 14 − 4 = 10, then take away 2 more: 10 − 2 = 8.

questions.prompt: Ravi has 9 marbles. He wants 15 marbles. How many MORE marbles does he need?

options.diagnosis: Added the two numbers in the problem instead of finding the missing part.
Counted the 9 itself while counting up to 15.
Stopped counting up one number too early.

questions.explanation: Count up from 9 to 15: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 — that is 6 jumps. So 9 + 6 = 15, and Ravi needs 6 more marbles.

nodes.title: Numbers up to 99: Tens and Ones
nodes.description: Big numbers are built from groups of ten. In the number 47, the 4 stands for 4 tens (forty) and the 7 stands for 7 ones. Once you can see tens and ones inside a number, you can read, write and compare any number up to 99.
learning_outcomes: Can count to 99 including across decade numbers (39 to 40, 59 to 60)
Can say how many tens and ones are in any 2-digit number
Can read and write 2-digit numbers from words and bundles
Can skip count by tens (10, 20, 30, ...)

misconceptions.description: Number words are transcribed literally: 'forty-two' becomes 402 (forty then two).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 402 for forty-two, 305 for thirty-five.
misconceptions.remedy: Use place-value (arrow) cards: the 40 card and the 2 card slide together so the 2 covers the 0. The child SEES why forty-two is two digits, not three.

misconceptions.description: Digits are just face values: the 4 in 47 means only 4, not 4 tens.
misconceptions.signal: Shows 47 with 4 counters and 7 counters; says 47 is '4 and 7, so 11'.
misconceptions.remedy: Build 47 from 4 bundles of ten sticks plus 7 loose sticks. Count the bundles aloud: '10, 20, 30, 40... 41, 42, ..., 47'. Repeat until 'the 4 means forty' is automatic.

misconceptions.description: Crossing a decade is a cliff: after 39 comes 'thirty-ten' or a jump to some other decade.
misconceptions.signal: Counts '...38, 39, 60...' or stalls completely at 39, 49, 69.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a 100-chart to show the pattern at every row end. With bundles: at 39, add one stick, bundle the 10 ones into a new ten — now there are 4 bundles, forty!

real_world_hooks: Bundles of ten sticks or straws
House numbers on a street
Pages of a storybook
Counting a pile of one-rupee coins into stacks of ten
teaching.video_search: tens and ones place value bundles grade 1

questions.prompt: How do we write the number forty-two?

options.diagnosis: Reversed the tens and ones digits.
Wrote the forty but dropped the two ones.

questions.explanation: Forty-two is 4 tens and 2 ones. The 2 sits in the ones place of 40, so we write 42 — just two digits.

questions.prompt: In the number 76, what does the digit 7 stand for?

options.diagnosis: Thinks each digit stands for the whole number.
Knows the word 'ones' but applied it to the tens place.

questions.explanation: In 76, the 7 is in the tens place, so it stands for 7 tens = 70. The 6 is in the ones place and stands for 6. Together: 70 + 6 = 76.

questions.prompt: Count on: 58, 59, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Jumped to the wrong decade after 59.
Went backwards to the start of the decade.

questions.explanation: After 59 we complete a new ten: 5 tens and 10 ones become 6 tens. So the next number is 60, and counting continues 61, 62, ...

nodes.title: Money: Recognising Coins and Notes
nodes.description: Money comes as coins and notes, and each one has a value printed on it — ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 and more. The value is what matters, not the size or the number of pieces. Knowing coins and notes lets us buy things and count small amounts.
learning_outcomes: Can name the common coins (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10) and notes (₹10, ₹20, ₹50)
Can compare two coins or notes by value using the printed number
Can find the total of two or three small coins and notes
Can show the same amount using different coins

misconceptions.description: More pieces of money means more money — five ₹1 coins feel worth more than one ₹10 coin.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses a handful of ₹1 coins over a single ₹10 coin; says 'I have more, I have five!'
misconceptions.remedy: Play exchange games at a pretend shop: trade ten ₹1 coins for one ₹10 coin and show both buy exactly the same toy. Count value, not pieces.

misconceptions.description: The physically bigger coin is worth more.
misconceptions.signal: Says a large old ₹1 coin beats a small ₹2 coin 'because it is bigger'.
misconceptions.remedy: Line up coins and read the printed number on each aloud. Sort the same coins two ways — by size and by value — and notice the orders are different.

misconceptions.description: Money is totalled by counting pieces, not by adding printed values.
misconceptions.signal: Holds a ₹10 note and a ₹2 coin and says 'I have 2 monies' or '₹2'.
misconceptions.remedy: Skip-count by the value printed on each piece: point to the note and say '10', then count on with the coin: '11, 12'. Practise with shopkeeper role-play.

real_world_hooks: Buying a toffee or pencil at the corner shop
Checking change with a parent after buying vegetables
Piggy bank (gullak) savings
Festival money from grandparents
teaching.video_search: indian coins and notes for kids recognising rupees grade 1

questions.prompt: Which of these coins has the MOST value: ₹1, ₹2 or ₹5?

options.diagnosis: May have picked the coin that looks biggest.

options.text: They are all worth the same
options.diagnosis: Treats every coin as just 'one coin'.

questions.explanation: The number printed on a coin tells its value. 5 is more than 2 and more than 1, so the ₹5 coin is worth the most — no matter what size it is.

questions.prompt: Ravi has one ₹10 note and one ₹2 coin. How much money does he have?

options.diagnosis: Counted 2 pieces of money instead of adding the values.
Doubled the ten instead of adding 10 and 2.
Wrote the values side by side instead of adding them.

questions.explanation: Start with the note: 10. Count on the coin's value: 11, 12. So Ravi has ₹12.

questions.prompt: Which of these is worth the SAME as one ₹10 coin?

options.diagnosis: Matched 'two coins' to 'ten' without adding the values (₹2 + ₹2 is only ₹4).
Five coins feel like a lot, but they total only ₹5.
Picked the single biggest coin without checking the total.

questions.explanation: Two ₹5 coins make 5 + 5 = 10, the same value as one ₹10 coin. The other choices total ₹4, ₹5 and ₹5 — all less than ₹10.

nodes.title: Shapes Around Us: Solids and Flat Shapes
nodes.description: Everything around us has a shape. Solid objects like balls, boxes and cans can roll, slide or stack, while flat shapes like circles, triangles, squares and rectangles live on paper and on the faces of solids. Naming and sorting shapes trains us to see the world like a mathematician.

chapters: What is Long, What is Round? (Shapes)

learning_outcomes: Can name circle, triangle, square and rectangle in any size or turn
Can sort everyday objects by whether they roll, slide or stack
Can tell a flat (2D) shape from a solid (3D) object
Can find shapes hiding in everyday things (a roti is round, a door is a rectangle)

misconceptions.description: A shape's name changes when it is turned — a tilted square becomes a 'diamond' and is no longer a square.
misconceptions.signal: Calls a square standing on its corner a diamond and insists it is not a square any more.
misconceptions.remedy: Rotate a square cut-out slowly in front of the child asking 'did any side change? any corner change?'. The shape is the same — only its position changed.

misconceptions.description: Flat-shape names are used for solid objects — a ball is a 'circle', a box is a 'square'.
misconceptions.signal: Points at a football and says 'circle'; calls a dice a square.
misconceptions.remedy: Dip the face of a solid in paint (or trace it) and stamp it on paper: the BOX prints a rectangle. The flat shape lives on the solid's face; the solid itself has its own name.

misconceptions.description: Shapes are judged by their typical look, not their properties — a long thin triangle 'isn't a triangle'.
misconceptions.signal: Rejects skinny, upside-down or slanted triangles; accepts only the classic equal-sided one pointing up.
misconceptions.remedy: Show many strange triangles and near-triangles (open corner, curved side). Decide together by counting: 3 straight sides and 3 corners — then it IS a triangle, however odd it looks.

real_world_hooks: Round rotis and square paneer pieces
A shape hunt around the house or classroom
Kites, doors, wheels and dice
Stacking boxes and rolling balls while packing
teaching.video_search: shapes around us solid shapes flat shapes grade 1 roll slide stack

questions.prompt: How many sides does a triangle have?

options.diagnosis: Confused the triangle with a square or rectangle.
Missed counting one side, often the bottom one.

questions.explanation: Every triangle — big, small, thin or tilted — has exactly 3 straight sides and 3 corners. That is what makes it a triangle!

questions.prompt: A square cut-out is turned so it stands on one corner. What is it now?

options.text: A diamond — not a square any more
A new shape called a kite

options.diagnosis: Focused only on the pointy corner at the top.

questions.explanation: Turning a shape does not change it. It still has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners, so it is still a square — just standing differently.

questions.prompt: Ria traces around one flat face of a cereal box on paper. What shape will she draw?

options.diagnosis: Gave the solid's name instead of the flat face's shape.
Does not connect the face of a solid with its flat outline.
Assumed every box face must be a square without looking at the long and short sides.

questions.explanation: A cereal box is a solid (a cuboid), but each flat face is a rectangle. Tracing a face draws that flat shape on the paper.

nodes.title: Comparing Length, Weight and Capacity
nodes.description: We compare things all the time: which pencil is longer, which bag is heavier, which glass holds more. To compare fairly we must line things up from the same end, feel or balance their weight, and pour to check what holds more. Careful comparing is the first step of all measurement.

chapters: What is Long, What is Round?

learning_outcomes: Can use the words longer/shorter, taller/shorter, heavier/lighter, holds more/holds less correctly
Can compare two lengths by lining objects up from the same end
Can guess and then check which of two objects is heavier
Can order three objects by length

misconceptions.description: Length is judged by where things end — the object sticking out farther is 'longer', even if the starting ends are not lined up.
misconceptions.signal: Says a shorter pencil placed ahead of a longer one is the longer pencil; ignores the starting ends.
misconceptions.remedy: Make a 'starting line' rule: both objects must touch the same baseline (a book edge) before comparing. Then deliberately offset objects and let the child catch the trick.

misconceptions.description: 'Big' means everything at once — bigger objects are assumed longer, heavier AND holding more.
misconceptions.signal: Uses 'big' for tall, heavy and full interchangeably; assumes the taller bottle must hold more water.
misconceptions.remedy: Set up surprises: a tall thin bottle vs a short wide pot — pour with cups and count. Insist on the precise words: longer, heavier, holds more.

misconceptions.description: The bigger-looking object is always heavier.
misconceptions.signal: Shocked that a small stone outweighs a big sponge or a bag of puffed rice.
misconceptions.remedy: Compare tricky pairs on a simple pan balance or in two hands: cotton pillow vs steel spoon. Predict first, test, then talk about the surprise.

real_world_hooks: Who is taller — you or your friend?
Carrying the shopping bags: which is heavier?
Which glass of lassi holds more?
Comparing chapati sizes at dinner
teaching.video_search: comparing length weight capacity grade 1 longer shorter heavier lighter

questions.prompt: Amma has a spoon and a broom. Which one is LONGER?

options.diagnosis: Mixed up the words longer and shorter.
Did not compare; may not picture the two objects side by side.

questions.explanation: Imagine them side by side, starting from the same end — the broom reaches much farther. The broom is longer. (Heavier does not mean longer!)

questions.prompt: Ria's ribbon is rolled up in a ball. Priya's ribbon lies straight. Priya says, 'Mine is longer because it LOOKS longer.' Is she right?

options.text: We can't tell yet — straighten both ribbons and line them up from the same end
Yes — the straight ribbon always is longer
Yes — rolling up a ribbon makes it shorter
options.diagnosis: Thinks changing the ribbon's position changes its length.

options.text: No — a rolled ribbon is always longer
options.diagnosis: Reversed the claim without any comparison.

questions.explanation: A ribbon keeps its length whether rolled or straight. To compare fairly, straighten both, put their starting ends together, and see which reaches farther.

questions.prompt: A big balloon and a small stone — which is heavier?

options.diagnosis: Guessed equality instead of comparing.

options.text: The balloon, because it is full
options.diagnosis: Judges weight by how big or full something looks.

questions.explanation: Bigger does not mean heavier! The balloon is mostly air and very light, while the little stone is solid and heavy. Hold one in each hand to feel it.

nodes.title: Time: Day, Night and Ordering Events
nodes.description: Our day has a rhythm: morning, afternoon, evening and night, and things happen in an order — we wake up before we go to school. Talking about before, after, day and night, and which activity takes longer is how we begin to understand time.

chapters: How do I Spend my Day (Time)

learning_outcomes: Can name the parts of the day (morning, afternoon, evening, night) and match activities to them
Can put 3-4 daily events in the right order using before and after
Can use yesterday, today and tomorrow correctly in conversation
Can say which of two activities takes longer

misconceptions.description: Duration is judged by feelings — boring things 'take hours' and fun things are 'quick', regardless of actual time.
misconceptions.signal: Insists tooth-brushing takes longer than a night's sleep, or that playtime lasted 'one minute'.
misconceptions.remedy: Time activities with a neutral measure the child controls: sand timer, counting claps or steps. Compare counts, then talk about why feelings fooled us.

misconceptions.description: The order and words of time are jumbled — yesterday/tomorrow used interchangeably, before/after swapped.
misconceptions.signal: Says 'tomorrow we went to the park'; puts wearing shoes before waking up when sequencing cards.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a picture strip of the child's own day and physically arrange the cards left to right each morning. Anchor yesterday/today/tomorrow to real, remembered events.

misconceptions.description: Day and night are defined by the child's own activities, not by the sun — nap time is 'night'.
misconceptions.signal: Calls an afternoon nap 'night'; thinks it becomes night whenever the curtains close.
misconceptions.remedy: Look outside together at different times and link day/night to the sun and moon. Discuss things that happen in daylight even while we sleep (afternoon nap).

real_world_hooks: Morning school bell and evening play time
The milkman comes in the morning, stars come at night
Getting ready: first uniform, then tiffin, then bus
Festival days: what did we do first?
teaching.video_search: parts of the day morning afternoon evening night sequencing events for kids

questions.prompt: Which of these do we usually do at NIGHT?

options.diagnosis: Breakfast belongs to the morning; daily order is jumbled.
Links the dark sky before sunrise with night-time activities.

questions.explanation: At night it is dark and our body rests — we sleep. Breakfast and school happen in the morning, and the sun rises to start the day.

questions.prompt: Put these in order: (a) wear the school uniform, (b) wake up, (c) reach school. Which happens FIRST?

options.text: They all happen at the same time
options.diagnosis: Does not yet see events as a sequence in time.

questions.explanation: First we wake up, then we wear the uniform, and after that we reach school. Waking up comes first — you cannot dress while asleep!

questions.prompt: Which takes LONGER: brushing your teeth, or a whole night's sleep?

options.diagnosis: Brushing feels long because it is boring, but feelings are not clocks.
Compared without thinking about the actual durations.
Does not yet see that any two activities' durations can be compared.

questions.explanation: Sleep lasts the whole night — many, many hours. Brushing takes only a few minutes, even when it feels long! We can compare how long things take, not just how they feel.

nodes.title: Repeating Patterns
nodes.description: A repeating pattern is made of a small unit that comes again and again, like red-blue, red-blue. If you can find the unit, you can say exactly what comes next — that is the power of a pattern. Spotting and extending patterns is the very beginning of algebraic thinking.
learning_outcomes: Can copy and extend a repeating pattern of colours, shapes, sounds or actions
Can point out the unit that repeats in a pattern
Can create an own repeating pattern and explain its rule
Can tell a real pattern from a random arrangement

misconceptions.description: A pattern is continued by repeating its LAST element, not its repeating unit.
misconceptions.signal: Extends red-blue-red-blue with blue, blue, blue — just copying the most recent item.
misconceptions.remedy: Circle or box the repeating unit ('red-blue') and chant it aloud like a beat. Extend one whole unit at a time, not one item at a time.

misconceptions.description: Any pretty or colourful arrangement is a 'pattern' — no rule is needed.
misconceptions.signal: Calls a random string of beads a pattern; cannot say what would come next.
misconceptions.remedy: Play 'pattern or not?': show a true pattern and a random string. The test: can you say for sure what comes next? If yes, it's a pattern; if not, it isn't.

misconceptions.description: In an ABB-type pattern the unit is misheard as AB — the doubled element gets counted once.
misconceptions.signal: Continues clap-stomp-stomp as clap-stomp, dropping the second stomp.
misconceptions.remedy: Do the pattern with the body and group the unit physically: jump into a hoop for each full unit. Draw loops around each complete unit before extending.

real_world_hooks: Rangoli and kolam designs at the doorstep
Border patterns on a sari or shawl
Clap-stomp body-beat games
Beads on a necklace, tiles on the floor
teaching.video_search: repeating patterns AB ABB for grade 1 kids find the unit

questions.prompt: Look at the pattern: red, blue, red, blue, red, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Repeated the last colour seen instead of following the unit.
Added any colour — treats the pattern as decoration without a rule.
Doubled an element instead of following the red-blue unit.

questions.explanation: The unit 'red-blue' repeats. After red comes blue, every single time. So the next colour is blue.

questions.prompt: A body pattern goes: clap, stomp, stomp, clap, stomp, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Doubled the wrong element of the unit.

questions.explanation: The repeating unit is clap-stomp-stomp. We have clap, stomp — so the unit still needs one more stomp before it starts again.

questions.prompt: In the pattern moon, star, star, moon, star, star — which part keeps repeating?

options.diagnosis: Ignored the moon; picked only the doubled element.
Picked the most noticeable item instead of the whole unit.

questions.explanation: The chunk 'moon-star-star' comes again and again. A pattern's unit is the WHOLE group that repeats, not just part of it.

nodes.title: Sorting and Classifying Objects
nodes.description: Sorting means putting things into groups by a rule — by colour, by shape, by size, or by what they are used for. The same objects can be sorted in different ways, but within one sort the rule must stay the same. Sorting is how we begin to organise information, the first step towards handling data.
learning_outcomes: Can sort a set of objects by a given rule (colour, shape, size, use)
Can state the rule used to sort a given group of objects
Can re-sort the same objects using a different rule
Can say which group has more or fewer objects after sorting

misconceptions.description: The sorting rule drifts midway — a colour sort quietly becomes a shape or type sort.
misconceptions.signal: The 'red things' pile suddenly contains a blue car 'because it is a car like the others'.
misconceptions.remedy: Say the rule aloud before starting and put a labelled rule card on each group. Check every object against the card: 'Is it red? Then it goes here — no other reason.'

misconceptions.description: Objects that don't obviously fit are left out — the child thinks some things 'belong nowhere'.
misconceptions.signal: Leaves items beside the piles saying 'this one doesn't go anywhere'.
misconceptions.remedy: Introduce an explicit 'others / not-red' group. Show that a good sort has a home for EVERY object — the rule splits everything, leaving nothing behind.

misconceptions.description: Groups are made by personal liking or stories, not by a shared attribute.
misconceptions.signal: Explains a group as 'these are my favourites' or 'the cow and goat are friends'.
misconceptions.remedy: Play guess-my-rule: sort objects silently and let the child work out the rule. Then ask about their groups: 'What is the SAME about everything in this pile?'

real_world_hooks: Sorting dal and rajma mixed in a bowl
Putting away toys: soft toys, blocks, cars
Sorting laundry by colour
Arranging the vegetable basket
teaching.video_search: sorting and classifying objects by attribute for grade 1

questions.prompt: You are sorting buttons by COLOUR. Where should a small red button go?

options.diagnosis: Switched from the colour rule to a size rule.

options.text: With the buttons you like best

questions.explanation: The rule is colour, so only colour matters. The button is red, so it joins the red pile — its size makes no difference for this sort.

questions.prompt: One box holds: a red bangle, a tomato and a red kite. What is the sorting rule?

options.diagnosis: Checked only the kite — the rule must fit every object.
Checked only the tomato and bangle; a kite is not round.

options.text: They are all found in the kitchen
options.diagnosis: Checked only the tomato; generalised from one item.

questions.explanation: A sorting rule must be true for EVERY object in the group. Toys? No — a tomato isn't a toy. Round? No — a kite isn't round. Red? Yes, all three are red!

questions.prompt: Sort these animals into two groups: cow, crow, goat, pigeon. Which way of grouping makes sense?

options.text: Birds (crow, pigeon) and four-legged animals (cow, goat)
Ones I like and ones I don't like
Cow with crow, because they are friends
options.diagnosis: Grouped by a story instead of a shared feature.

options.text: Each animal in its own group
options.diagnosis: Could not find a feature the animals share.

questions.explanation: A useful sort uses a feature we can check: crows and pigeons both fly and have wings; cows and goats both walk on four legs. Everyone can see and agree on the rule.

nodes.title: Place Value: Comparing and Ordering to 99
nodes.description: A digit's value depends on WHERE it sits: in 47, the 4 means forty. To compare two numbers we look at the tens first, and only if the tens match do we check the ones. This lets us order any set of numbers up to 99 with certainty.
learning_outcomes: Can write any 2-digit number in expanded form (47 = 40 + 7)
Can compare two 2-digit numbers by checking tens first, then ones
Can order three or more numbers from smallest to greatest and greatest to smallest
Can find the number that is 1 more, 1 less, 10 more or 10 less than a given number

misconceptions.description: Numbers are compared by their biggest digit anywhere — 29 beats 41 'because 9 is bigger'.
misconceptions.signal: Picks the number with the larger ones digit as greater; compares ones before tens.
misconceptions.remedy: Build both numbers with bundles of ten: 4 bundles beat 2 bundles before loose sticks even matter. Then locate both on a 100-chart — the later number is greater.

misconceptions.description: Digits are read at face value, so numbers with the same digits are 'the same' — 47 and 74 are equal.
misconceptions.signal: Says 47 = 74 'because both have a 4 and a 7'; adds digits to compare sizes.
misconceptions.remedy: Build 47 and 74 side by side with tens-bundles and ones. Seeing 4 bundles versus 7 bundles makes the difference between the two numbers physical and obvious.

misconceptions.description: Tens and ones swap when writing from words — 'six tens and two ones' becomes 26.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 26 for six tens and two ones; reads 71 as seventeen.
misconceptions.remedy: Always read numbers left to right with a place-value mat: point to the tens column and say the tens first. Use arrow cards to compose the number physically.

real_world_hooks: Comparing cricket scores of two teams
House numbers and bus route numbers
Whose granny is older?
Prices of two toys in a shop
teaching.video_search: comparing 2 digit numbers tens and ones place value grade 2

questions.prompt: Which number is bigger: 34 or 43?

options.diagnosis: Compared the ones digits (4 > 3) instead of the tens.
Compared by position on the page, not by value.

questions.explanation: Check tens first: 43 has 4 tens (40), while 34 has only 3 tens (30). So 43 is bigger — the same digits in different places make different numbers.

questions.prompt: Which number has 6 tens and 2 ones?

options.diagnosis: Added the digits 6 + 2 instead of using place value.
Wrote 60 and 2 side by side instead of combining them.

questions.explanation: 6 tens make 60, and 2 ones make 2. Together: 60 + 2 = 62. The tens digit is written first.

questions.prompt: Arrange from SMALLEST to BIGGEST: 58, 85, 79.

options.diagnosis: Ordered correctly but from biggest to smallest — read the direction again.
Ordered by the ones digits (5, 8, 9) instead of comparing tens first.
No consistent comparing rule — likely guessed.

questions.explanation: Compare tens: 58 has 5 tens, 79 has 7 tens, 85 has 8 tens. So smallest to biggest is 58, 79, 85.

nodes.title: Numbers up to 999: Hundreds
nodes.description: After tens come hundreds: ten tens bundle into one hundred. A 3-digit number like 407 has hundreds, tens and ones — and a zero can hold a place to show 'no tens'. With hundreds we can count, read and compare numbers all the way to 999.
learning_outcomes: Can explain that 10 tens make 1 hundred
Can read and write 3-digit numbers from words and from hundreds-tens-ones
Can write a 3-digit number in expanded form (263 = 200 + 60 + 3)
Can compare and order 3-digit numbers by checking hundreds first

misconceptions.description: Number words are transcribed piece by piece — 'two hundred sixty-three' becomes 200603 or 2063.
misconceptions.signal: Written numbers grow extra digits whenever the child writes from dictation.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a hundreds-tens-ones place mat with arrow cards: 200, 60 and 3 slide on top of each other to make 263. Three places, three digits — never more.

misconceptions.description: Zero as a placeholder is dropped or misplaced — 'four hundred seven' becomes 47 or 4007.
misconceptions.signal: Internal zeros vanish (47) or multiply (4007) when writing numbers with empty places.
misconceptions.remedy: On the place mat, point at the empty tens column: 'no tens — but the place still needs a digit'. Write 0 as the place-holder and read the number back together.

misconceptions.description: Numbers are compared by their most impressive digits, not by place — 389 beats 400 'because 8 and 9 are big'.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses 389 > 400; ignores the hundreds digit when the other digits look large.
misconceptions.remedy: Build both numbers with hundreds-squares, tens-rods and ones: 4 flat hundreds beat 3 flat hundreds no matter what loose pieces come after. Hundreds first, always.

real_world_hooks: Counting 100-rupee notes
Pages in a fat storybook
Runs in a full day of test cricket
School attendance: how many children in all classes?
teaching.video_search: 3 digit numbers hundreds tens ones place value grade 2

questions.prompt: Write 'two hundred sixty-three' in figures.

options.diagnosis: Wrote 200 then 63 side by side.
Swapped the tens and ones digits.

questions.explanation: Two hundred sixty-three = 200 + 60 + 3. The digits stack into three places: 2 hundreds, 6 tens, 3 ones — 263.

questions.prompt: Which of these is 'four hundred seven'?

options.diagnosis: Added extra zeros instead of one placeholder zero.
Put the 7 in the tens place instead of the ones place.

questions.explanation: Four hundred seven has 4 hundreds, NO tens, and 7 ones. The zero holds the empty tens place: 407.

questions.prompt: Which is the GREATEST: 389, 400 or 398?

options.diagnosis: Chose the number with the biggest-looking digits (8 and 9).
Compared only the number of digits, not their values.

questions.explanation: Compare hundreds first: 400 has 4 hundreds; the others have only 3. So 400 is greatest, even though its other digits are zeros.

nodes.title: 2-digit Addition and Subtraction with Regrouping
nodes.description: When we add and the ones spill over ten, we bundle them into a new ten — that is carrying. When we subtract and the ones are not enough, we open up a ten — that is borrowing. Regrouping lets us add and subtract any numbers up to 99 quickly and correctly.
learning_outcomes: Can add two 2-digit numbers with and without carrying
Can subtract 2-digit numbers with and without borrowing
Can explain regrouping using bundles of tens and ones
Can check an answer using estimation or the opposite operation
Can solve one-step story problems involving 2-digit addition and subtraction

misconceptions.description: Each column is added separately and all digits are written down — 37 + 25 becomes 512 (5 tens, 12 ones).
misconceptions.signal: Answers have too many digits; the ones column shows a two-digit number.
misconceptions.remedy: Add with base-ten blocks: when 12 ones appear, physically exchange 10 of them for one ten-rod BEFORE writing anything. Ten ones can never stay in the ones place.

misconceptions.description: In each column the smaller digit is subtracted from the larger, whatever their position — 52 − 38 gives 26.
misconceptions.signal: Never borrows; every column shows top-minus-bottom or bottom-minus-top, whichever 'works'.
misconceptions.remedy: Build 52 with blocks and try to remove 8 ones — you must break open a ten first. Also estimate: 52 − 38 is about 50 − 40, so an answer near 26 can't be right.

misconceptions.description: The carried ten is written and then forgotten — it never gets added into the tens column.
misconceptions.signal: Answers are exactly 10 less than correct on carrying problems (48 + 34 = 72).
misconceptions.remedy: Make the carry loud and physical: place the exchanged ten-rod ON the tens pile and count it first: '1 ten (carried) + 4 + 3'. In writing, circle the carry digit until the habit sticks.

real_world_hooks: Adding runs of two batsmen in cricket
Money: buying two things and finding what's left of ₹50
Counting total children in two classes
Train seats filled and empty
teaching.video_search: 2 digit addition subtraction regrouping carrying borrowing grade 2

questions.prompt: What is 37 + 25?

options.diagnosis: Added 7 + 5 = 12, wrote 2, but forgot to carry the ten.
Small counting slip in the ones; method likely fine.

questions.explanation: Ones: 7 + 5 = 12 — write 2, carry 1 ten. Tens: 3 + 2 + 1 (carried) = 6. Answer: 62.

questions.prompt: What is 52 − 38?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in each column (8 − 2, 5 − 3).
Borrowed for the ones but forgot to reduce the tens digit.
Added instead of subtracting.

questions.explanation: Ones: 2 is less than 8, so borrow a ten: 12 − 8 = 4. Tens: 4 − 3 = 1. Answer: 14. Check: 14 + 38 = 52. ✓

questions.prompt: Rahul had 45 marbles. He won 28 more in a game. How many marbles does he have now?

options.diagnosis: Forgot to add the carried ten.
Subtracted instead of adding — 'won more' means the total grows.

questions.explanation: 45 + 28: ones 5 + 8 = 13 — write 3, carry 1. Tens: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. Rahul now has 73 marbles.

nodes.title: Multiplication as Equal Groups and Repeated Addition
nodes.description: Multiplication is a shortcut for adding the same number again and again. '3 × 4' means 3 equal groups of 4 — like 3 plates with 4 laddoos each — and equals 4 + 4 + 4. Arrays of rows and columns show why 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 give the same total.
learning_outcomes: Can describe a multiplication like 3 × 4 as '3 groups of 4'
Can write repeated addition (5 + 5 + 5) as multiplication (3 × 5) and back
Can find totals of equal groups by skip counting
Can arrange objects in rows and columns (arrays) and count them two ways

misconceptions.description: The × sign works like +: 3 × 4 is answered as 7.
misconceptions.signal: Answers to multiplication facts equal the sum of the factors.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the groups every time at first: 3 circles with 4 dots each. Count the dots — 12, not 7. The 3 counts GROUPS, the 4 counts what's IN each group; they are different jobs.

misconceptions.description: Groups need not be equal — any 3 groups 'of about 4' can be multiplied.
misconceptions.signal: Draws groups of 3, 5 and 4 for 3 × 4; happily 'multiplies' unequal shares.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort picture cards into 'can multiply' (equal groups) and 'cannot multiply yet' (unequal). Multiplication's superpower only works when every group is exactly the same size.

misconceptions.description: 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 are unrelated problems that might have different totals.
misconceptions.signal: Solves 3 × 4, then starts counting from scratch for 4 × 3; is unsure the answers match.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a 3-by-4 array of buttons and simply rotate it a quarter turn: the same buttons show 4 rows of 3. Same array, same total — order doesn't change the answer.

real_world_hooks: Idlis served 3 per plate
Egg trays with equal rows
Wheels on 5 autos: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3
Chocolate bars broken into equal rows
teaching.video_search: multiplication as equal groups repeated addition arrays grade 2

questions.prompt: There are 3 plates. Each plate has 4 laddoos. How many laddoos in all?

options.diagnosis: Added 3 + 4 instead of finding 3 groups of 4.
Wrote the two numbers side by side.
Skip-counting slip: 4, 8, ... lost track on the last group.

questions.explanation: 3 groups of 4: count 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, or skip count 4, 8, 12. So 3 × 4 = 12 laddoos.

questions.prompt: Which of these means the SAME as 5 + 5 + 5?

options.diagnosis: Used the repeated number for both factors; forgot to COUNT how many fives.
Turned every plus sign into a multiplication sign.

questions.explanation: 5 + 5 + 5 is three fives. 'Three fives' is written 3 × 5. Count the groups (3) and say what is in each group (5).

questions.prompt: Meena arranges 4 rows of 6 chairs. Ravi arranges 6 rows of 4 chairs. Who uses more chairs?

options.text: You must count each arrangement separately to know
options.diagnosis: Does not yet trust that order doesn't change the total.

questions.explanation: Turn Meena's arrangement sideways and it becomes Ravi's! 4 × 6 = 24 and 6 × 4 = 24. Changing the order of multiplication never changes the total.

nodes.title: Money: Simple Totals and Change
nodes.description: Shopping is maths in action: we add prices to find the total, and when we pay with a bigger note, we get change — the difference between what we gave and what it cost. We can also make the same amount in many ways using different coins and notes.
learning_outcomes: Can add two or three prices to find a total up to ₹99
Can work out the change from ₹10, ₹20 or ₹50
Can make a given amount using different combinations of coins and notes
Can check whether the money offered is enough to buy something

misconceptions.description: Money is totalled by counting pieces, not values — 3 notes means ₹3.
misconceptions.signal: Reports the number of coins/notes as the amount; ₹10 + ₹5 becomes '2 rupees'.
misconceptions.remedy: Skip-count by each denomination's value in shop play: '10... 15'. Have the child be the shopkeeper who must catch customers 'paying' with the wrong count.

misconceptions.description: Change is found by ADDING the price and the payment.
misconceptions.signal: For a ₹7 toffee paid with ₹10, announces change of ₹17; change comes out bigger than the note given.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the count-up method with real coins: start at the price (7) and count up to the payment (8, 9, 10) — the coins you added ARE the change. Sanity-check: change must be SMALLER than what you handed over.

misconceptions.description: You can only pay if you have the exact single note or coin matching the price.
misconceptions.signal: Stuck when asked to pay ₹15 while holding a ₹10 and a ₹5; says 'I don't have a fifteen'.
misconceptions.remedy: Play 'make it many ways': build ₹15 with 10+5, 5+5+5, 10+2+2+1. Every combination buys the same toy — the total value is what pays, not any single piece.

real_world_hooks: Buying vegetables at the sabzi mandi
Paying the bus or auto fare
School canteen: samosa and juice, what's the total?
Checking change at the kirana shop
teaching.video_search: adding money finding change indian rupees grade 2

questions.prompt: A pencil costs ₹6 and an eraser costs ₹4. How much for both together?

options.diagnosis: Counted 2 items — or subtracted — instead of adding the prices.
Wrote the two prices side by side.
Addition slip of one; recheck 6 + 4.

questions.explanation: Add the prices: ₹6 + ₹4 = ₹10. Together they cost ten rupees — exactly one ₹10 note.

questions.prompt: A toffee costs ₹7. You give the shopkeeper a ₹10 note. How much change should you get back?

options.diagnosis: Counted up but included 7 itself as a step.
Confused the change with the price.

questions.explanation: Count up from 7 to 10: 8, 9, 10 — that's ₹3. Change = what you gave (₹10) minus the cost (₹7) = ₹3.

questions.prompt: A kite costs ₹12. Which of these pays EXACTLY ₹12?

options.diagnosis: That makes ₹15 — didn't check the total against the price.
Two coins showing '2' don't make twelve — that is only ₹4.
Matched the digits 1 and 2 of 'twelve' instead of the value — that is only ₹3.

questions.explanation: ₹10 + ₹2 = ₹12, exactly the price. The other combinations make ₹15, ₹4 and ₹3 — either too much or too little.

nodes.title: 2D and 3D Shapes: Faces, Edges, Lines
nodes.description: Solid shapes like cubes, cuboids, cylinders and spheres have faces you can touch, edges you can run a finger along, and corners that poke. Flat shapes live on the faces of solids. Learning to count faces, edges and corners — and to tell straight lines from curves — makes us precise about shapes.
learning_outcomes: Can name cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone and sphere from real objects
Can count the faces, edges and corners of a cube or cuboid
Can predict the flat shape a solid's face will print or trace
Can tell straight lines from curved lines and draw both

misconceptions.description: Only the faces visible in a picture exist — a cube 'has 3 faces'.
misconceptions.signal: Counts faces from a drawing and reports 3 for a cube or cuboid.
misconceptions.remedy: Hand the child a real box and a sheet of stickers: stick one sticker on every face while counting. Turning the box reveals the hidden faces — six stickers, every time.

misconceptions.description: Flat and solid shape names are interchangeable — a cube IS a square, a ball IS a circle.
misconceptions.signal: Says 'the dice is a square'; calls a can a circle.
misconceptions.remedy: Press solids onto an ink pad or trace their faces: the CUBE prints a square, but you can't put the cube in your pocket flat! The solid and its face-print get different names.

misconceptions.description: Edges and corners are the same thing — counting one when asked for the other.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 8 when asked how many edges a cube has (counted corners), or vice versa.
misconceptions.remedy: Give each its own action: RUN a finger along an edge ('a road'), PINCH a corner ('a point that pokes'). Do the actions while counting so the words attach to different experiences.

real_world_hooks: Dice, bricks, laddoos and tin cans
Footprints and stamp printing with vegetables
Ice cream cones and cricket balls
Railway tracks: straight lines; bangles: curves
teaching.video_search: faces edges corners of 3d shapes grade 2 solids around us

questions.prompt: How many faces does a dice (cube) have?

options.diagnosis: Counted only the faces visible in a picture.
Thought of a square's 4 sides instead of the cube's faces.
Counted the corners instead of the faces.

questions.explanation: A cube has 6 flat faces — top, bottom, and 4 around the sides. That's why dice show the numbers 1 to 6!

questions.prompt: A brick is shaped like which solid?

options.diagnosis: Named the flat face instead of the solid.
Close — but a cube's faces are all equal squares, while a brick is longer than it is wide.
A cylinder has curved sides and round ends; a brick has flat faces.

questions.explanation: A brick is a cuboid — a box shape with 6 flat rectangular faces. 'Rectangle' names only a flat face, not the whole solid.

questions.prompt: Sita dips the round bottom of a tin can in paint and presses it on paper. What shape does it print?

options.diagnosis: Gave the solid's name; the print shows only the flat face.
Thought of the can's curved side rolled out, not its bottom face.
Pictured the tilted view of a can in drawings; a straight-down print is a true circle.

questions.explanation: The flat bottom of a can is a circle, so it prints a circle. The can itself is a cylinder — the print only shows one face.

nodes.title: Measuring Length: Non-standard to Standard Units
nodes.description: We can measure length with handspans, footsteps or pencils — but everyone's hands and feet are different, so the counts don't match. That is why the world agreed on standard units like the centimetre and metre. Measuring means laying units end to end with no gaps and no overlaps, then counting them.

chapters: What is Long, What is Round?

learning_outcomes: Can measure a length by repeating a unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps
Can explain why different people get different handspan counts for the same object
Can say why standard units like centimetre and metre are needed
Can measure short lengths in centimetres with a ruler

misconceptions.description: The measured object 'changes size' when different units give different counts — or non-standard and standard units are equally reliable for sharing results.
misconceptions.signal: Puzzled that the table is '7 spans for me but 5 for Papa'; concludes the table changed or someone measured wrong.
misconceptions.remedy: Measure one object with the child's hand, an adult's hand, and a rope of fixed length. Discuss: the table never changed — the UNITS differed. That's exactly why shops and tailors use the same metre everywhere.

misconceptions.description: Units can be laid with gaps or overlaps and the count still measures the length.
misconceptions.signal: Places paper clips with spaces between them, or overlapping, and confidently reports the count.
misconceptions.remedy: Make a 'unit train' rule: each unit must touch the next, nose to tail, along a straight line. Compare a gappy measurement with a snug one on the same object and see the counts disagree.

misconceptions.description: A bigger unit gives a bigger count — measuring in metres should give more than in handspans.
misconceptions.signal: Predicts the blackboard will be 'more metres than handspans' because metres are bigger.
misconceptions.remedy: Measure the same length in both units and record the two counts. Talk it through: bigger steps means FEWER steps to cross the room — the bigger the unit, the smaller the count.

real_world_hooks: The tailor measuring cloth with a metre tape
Measuring your bed in handspans, then with a tape
Long jump distances on sports day
How many footsteps across the classroom?
teaching.video_search: measuring length non standard units handspan why we need standard units grade 2

questions.prompt: Which of these is a STANDARD unit of length — the same for everybody?

options.diagnosis: Handspans differ from person to person, so they are not standard.
A cup measures how much something holds, not how long it is.
Kilograms measure weight, not length.

questions.explanation: A centimetre is exactly the same length everywhere in the world — that's what makes it standard. Handspans change with the person, and cups and kilograms measure different things.

questions.prompt: Meena measures the table with her handspan and gets 7. Her father measures the same table and gets 5. Why?

options.text: Father's handspan is longer, so fewer spans are needed

options.diagnosis: Assumes different counts mean a mistake, not different units.

options.text: Bigger hands always give bigger counts

questions.explanation: The table stayed the same — the units differed! A longer handspan covers more table at each step, so fewer are needed. This is exactly why we need standard units like the metre.

questions.prompt: Anu and Ben each measure the same rope with cubes. Anu leaves gaps between her cubes. Ben places his touching each other. Whose count measures the rope correctly?

options.text: Ben — units must touch, with no gaps
Both are right — any way of laying units works
Neither — you can only measure with a ruler
options.diagnosis: Over-restricts measuring to one tool; repeated units measure perfectly well.

questions.explanation: The units must cover the whole rope end to end, with no gaps and no overlaps. Anu's gaps hide bits of rope that never got counted, so her count is too small.

nodes.title: Weight and Capacity: Comparing and Measuring
nodes.description: Weight tells how heavy something is; capacity tells how much a container can hold. A balance shows which of two things is heavier — the heavier side goes down. To compare containers fairly, we fill them using the same cup and count. Looks can trick us: big things can be light, and tall containers can hold less.
learning_outcomes: Can compare two objects' weights using hands or a simple balance
Can read a pan balance: the heavier side goes down
Can compare two containers' capacities by filling with a common cup and counting
Can order three objects by weight or three containers by capacity

misconceptions.description: The bigger-looking object is always the heavier one.
misconceptions.signal: Ranks a large empty carton above a small brick; judges parcels only by size.
misconceptions.remedy: Weigh surprise pairs on a balance: big sponge vs small stone, puffed-rice packet vs iron lock. Predict, test, discuss — size and weight are different properties.

misconceptions.description: The taller container holds more, no matter how thin it is.
misconceptions.signal: Picks the tall slim bottle over the short wide pot without testing.
misconceptions.remedy: Fill both containers using the same cup and count cupfuls. Then pour water from the tall bottle into the wide pot to SEE it fit with room to spare.

misconceptions.description: On a balance, the side that rises holds the heavier object.
misconceptions.signal: Points at the raised pan and says 'this side wins, it went up — it's heavier'.
misconceptions.remedy: Connect to the see-saw: the heavier friend sinks down! Let the child sit on a see-saw or hold heavy vs light bags in outstretched hands — the heavy one pulls DOWN.

real_world_hooks: The sabziwala's balance and weights
See-saw in the park
Filling water bottles from a jug
Which shopping bag is heavier to carry?
teaching.video_search: comparing weight capacity balance scale pouring for grade 2

questions.prompt: On a balance, the pan with the mango goes DOWN and the pan with the ball goes UP. Which is heavier?

options.diagnosis: If they weighed the same, the pans would stay level.

questions.explanation: On a balance, the heavier thing pulls its pan DOWN — just like the heavier child on a see-saw. The mango's pan went down, so the mango is heavier.

questions.prompt: A big soft pillow and a small iron lock — which is heavier?

options.diagnosis: Guessed equality instead of thinking about the materials.

options.text: You cannot compare such different things
options.diagnosis: Any two objects can be compared by weight — hold one in each hand!

questions.explanation: Bigger doesn't mean heavier! The pillow is full of soft, light stuffing, while iron is heavy even in small pieces. A balance would dip on the lock's side.

questions.prompt: Ria fills a tall thin bottle with 4 cups of water. She fills a short wide pot with 6 cups. Which holds more?

options.text: The tall thin bottle — it is taller

options.diagnosis: Ignored the cup counts of 4 and 6.

options.text: You can't tell by counting cups
options.diagnosis: Counting equal cupfuls is exactly how we compare capacity fairly.

questions.explanation: The same cup was used for both, so we can compare the counts: 6 cups is more than 4 cups. The short wide pot holds more, even though the bottle is taller.

nodes.title: Time: Days, Months, Calendar and O'Clock
nodes.description: The 7 days of the week go round and round like a wheel, and the 12 months fill a year on the calendar. A clock has two hands: the short hand tells the hour, and when the long hand points to 12, it is exactly o'clock. Reading calendars and clocks helps us plan our days.
learning_outcomes: Can say the days of the week in order and name yesterday/tomorrow for any day
Can name the 12 months in order and find dates on a calendar
Can read o'clock times on a clock with hands
Can tell which hand of a clock shows hours and which shows minutes

misconceptions.description: Weeks, months and years blur together — 'a week has 30 days', 'a month has 7 days'.
misconceptions.signal: Mixes up how many days are in a week versus a month; counts months on a week chart.
misconceptions.remedy: Keep a real calendar in view daily. Circle one full week in one colour and one full month in another; count the days inside each loop together.

misconceptions.description: The clock's hands are read the wrong way round — the long hand is taken as the hour.
misconceptions.signal: For 4 o'clock (short hand on 4, long on 12) reads '12 o'clock'.
misconceptions.remedy: Start with a one-handed clock showing only the short hour hand. Once hour-reading is secure, add the long hand and its special o'clock position at 12.

misconceptions.description: The week has an edge — after Sunday (or Saturday) the days 'run out'.
misconceptions.signal: Cannot answer 'what comes after Saturday?'; treats the week list as a line that ends.
misconceptions.remedy: Make a circular week wheel the child can spin: after Saturday comes Sunday, then Monday again, forever. Chant the cycle past the 'edge' several times.

real_world_hooks: Finding your birthday on the calendar
School timetable: which day is PT?
Sunday — the no-school day!
Festival dates: when is Diwali this year?
teaching.video_search: days of the week months calendar reading o'clock grade 2

questions.prompt: How many days are there in one week?

options.diagnosis: Counted only the school days.
Gave the days in a month instead of a week.
Gave the number of months in a year.

questions.explanation: A week has 7 days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. School days plus the weekend make all seven!

questions.prompt: On a clock, the SHORT hand points to 4 and the LONG hand points to 12. What time is it?

options.diagnosis: Read the long hand as the hour hand.
Read the hour hand at the next number instead of the one it points to.
The long hand at 12 means exactly o'clock; at half past it would point to 6.

questions.explanation: The SHORT hand tells the hour: it points to 4. The LONG hand on 12 means it is exactly on the hour. So it is 4 o'clock.

questions.prompt: Today is Saturday. What day will it be tomorrow?

options.diagnosis: Went one day backwards — that was yesterday.
Skipped over Sunday, jumping straight to the next school day.

options.text: There is no day after Saturday

questions.explanation: The days go round like a wheel: ...Friday, Saturday, SUNDAY, Monday... After Saturday always comes Sunday — the week never runs out!

nodes.title: Growing Patterns in Numbers and Shapes
nodes.description: Some patterns don't repeat — they GROW. A staircase gains a step each time; the numbers 2, 4, 6, 8 climb by 2 at every jump. To continue a growing pattern you must find its rule: what changes from one step to the next, and by how much?
learning_outcomes: Can continue a number pattern that grows by the same amount each time
Can build and extend growing shape patterns (staircases, triangles of dots)
Can state the rule of a growing pattern in words ('add 5 each time')
Can check whether a claimed rule works for EVERY step of a pattern

misconceptions.description: A growing pattern is treated like a repeating one — the sequence starts over instead of growing.
misconceptions.signal: Continues 2, 4, 6 with 2, 4, 6 again; rebuilds the same staircase step instead of a taller one.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the pattern with blocks so growth is physical: each staircase step NEEDS more blocks. Compare a repeating pattern and a growing one side by side and name the difference.

misconceptions.description: The pattern is seen but the rule is not — the next term is guessed instead of computed from the constant jump.
misconceptions.signal: Continues 2, 4, 6, 8 with 9; says 'the numbers get bigger' but cannot say by how much.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw jump arrows between consecutive terms and write the jump size on each arrow: +2, +2, +2. The rule is the number ON the arrows, and the next term comes from one more identical jump.

misconceptions.description: The rule may change midway if it makes an answer 'fit' — patterns don't need one consistent rule.
misconceptions.signal: Justifies a wrong next term by inventing a new rule for the last step only ('here it adds 3 instead').
misconceptions.remedy: Play convince-me: any claimed rule must be tested against EVERY given step. If the rule breaks anywhere, it isn't the pattern's rule.

real_world_hooks: Staircase steps getting taller
Rangoli dots growing ring by ring
Saving ₹5 more each week in the gullak
Rows in a wedding-hall seating: each row longer
teaching.video_search: growing patterns numbers shapes find the rule grade 2

questions.prompt: Continue the pattern: 2, 4, 6, 8, ___?

options.diagnosis: Started the sequence over instead of growing it.
Added 1 — didn't find the jump size of 2.
Jumped by 4 — skipped one step of the pattern.

questions.explanation: Each number jumps up by 2: 2 → 4 → 6 → 8. One more jump of 2 gives 10.

questions.prompt: A staircase pattern uses 1 block, then 3 blocks, then 5 blocks. How many blocks will the next step need?

options.diagnosis: Repeated the last step instead of growing.
Added 1 instead of the pattern's jump of 2.
Jumped two steps ahead — 9 comes after 7.

questions.explanation: The steps grow by 2 each time: 1, 3, 5, ... so the next step needs 5 + 2 = 7 blocks.

questions.prompt: What is the rule of the pattern 5, 10, 15, 20?

options.diagnosis: True but not a rule — it can't tell us the NEXT number.

questions.explanation: Check every jump: 5→10 is +5, 10→15 is +5, 15→20 is +5. The rule 'add 5 each time' works at every single step — so the next number must be 25.

nodes.title: Pictographs: Recording and Reading Data
nodes.description: A pictograph shows information using little pictures — one picture for each thing counted (or sometimes for two or more). Lining the pictures up in neat rows lets us see at a glance which group has most and how many more. Pictographs turn messy counts into a story our eyes can read.
learning_outcomes: Can collect simple data by counting and record it with tally marks or pictures
Can read how many each row of a pictograph shows
Can answer most/least and how-many-more questions from a pictograph
Can use a key where one symbol stands for more than one object

misconceptions.description: Rows are compared by how LONG they look, not by how many symbols they hold.
misconceptions.signal: Picks a row with 3 widely-spaced big pictures over a row with 5 small tight ones as 'more'.
misconceptions.remedy: Use grid paper so every symbol takes exactly one cell — then length and count agree. Deliberately show a spaced-out short row and count together to expose the trick.

misconceptions.description: The key is ignored — each symbol always counts as exactly one.
misconceptions.signal: With a key of 1 picture = 2 books, reports 3 pictures as 3 books.
misconceptions.remedy: Act the key out physically: for each symbol, place 2 real books on the table. Count the books, not the symbols. Start with 1:1 charts, then re-draw the SAME data with a 1:2 key.

misconceptions.description: Questions about the data are answered from personal preference or memory, not from the chart.
misconceptions.signal: Says 'most children like mango because I like mango' without looking at the rows.
misconceptions.remedy: Require pointing: every answer must come with a finger on the row that proves it. Ask 'where does the CHART say that?' until checking becomes habit.

real_world_hooks: Favourite fruit survey of the class
How the class comes to school: walk, cycle, bus
Runs scored by each friend in gully cricket
Counting birds visiting the window each morning
teaching.video_search: pictograph for kids reading picture graphs with key grade 2

questions.prompt: Fruit chart — Mango: ●●●●, Banana: ●●, Apple: ●●●. Each ● = 1 child. How many children chose apple?

options.diagnosis: Read the banana row instead of the apple row.
Read the mango row — the longest one — instead of the row asked about.
Added up all the rows instead of reading just the apple row.

questions.explanation: Find the apple row and count its symbols: ●●● = 3. Three children chose apple.

questions.prompt: In the same chart (Mango ●●●●, Banana ●●, Apple ●●●), which fruit did MOST children choose?

options.diagnosis: May have answered with a personal favourite instead of reading the chart.
Chose the LEAST popular row — misread 'most' as 'least'.
The chart tells us exactly — compare the symbol counts.

questions.explanation: Count each row: mango 4, apple 3, banana 2. Mango has the most symbols, so most children chose mango — whatever OUR favourite may be!

questions.prompt: In another chart, each ● stands for 2 books. Rani's row shows ●●●. How many books does Rani have?

options.diagnosis: Counted the symbols and ignored the key.
Added 3 symbols + 2 from the key instead of multiplying.
Doubled the symbols and then added the key again (3 × 2 + 2).

questions.explanation: The key says each ● = 2 books. Three symbols mean 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 books. Always check the key before counting!

nodes.title: 4-digit Numbers and Place Value
nodes.description: With four places — thousands, hundreds, tens and ones — we can name every number up to 9999. Each step left multiplies a digit's value by ten, and a zero holds any empty place. Reading, writing, expanding and comparing 4-digit numbers makes big numbers as friendly as small ones.
learning_outcomes: Can read and write 4-digit numbers from words and figures
Can give the place value of any digit in a 4-digit number
Can write a 4-digit number in expanded form (3206 = 3000 + 200 + 6)
Can compare and order 4-digit numbers
Can find 1, 10, 100 or 1000 more or less than a given number

misconceptions.description: Number words are written down literally — 'three thousand two hundred six' becomes 3000200 6 or 32006.
misconceptions.signal: Written numbers sprout extra digits when taken from dictation; expanded parts get chained together.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a Th | H | T | O place mat: four places means at most four digits. Compose with arrow cards (3000, 200, 6 slide together into 3206) so the compression is visible.

misconceptions.description: Digits are compared at face value, ignoring place — 4999 beats 5001 'because it has three 9s'.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses the number with the most impressive digits as greater; says the 7 in 4738 'is just 7'.
misconceptions.remedy: Compare from the LEFT: thousands first. Build both numbers with thousand-blocks — five loose thousands beat four thousands however shiny the leftover digits are.

misconceptions.description: Placeholder zeros are dropped or shuffled — 'three thousand two hundred six' becomes 326 or 3260.
misconceptions.signal: Numbers with internal zeros collapse (326) or the zero drifts to another place (3260).
misconceptions.remedy: Say each place aloud while pointing at the mat: '3 thousands, 2 hundreds, NO tens — write 0 to hold the place — 6 ones.' Practise dictation of zero-rich numbers (4056, 7009).

real_world_hooks: Prices of bicycles and phones in rupees
Train numbers and PIN codes
Populations of villages
Years on a timeline: 2026 is a 4-digit number!
teaching.video_search: 4 digit numbers place value expanded form grade 3

questions.prompt: Write 'three thousand two hundred six' in figures.

options.diagnosis: Dropped the placeholder zero in the tens place.
Put the 6 in the tens place; the zero must hold the tens, not the ones.

questions.explanation: 3 thousands, 2 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones: 3000 + 200 + 0 + 6 = 3206. The zero holds the empty tens place.

questions.prompt: What is the VALUE of the digit 7 in 4738?

options.diagnosis: Gave the face value; ignored the hundreds place it sits in.
Placed the 7 one position too far right (tens instead of hundreds).
Placed the 7 one position too far left (thousands instead of hundreds).

questions.explanation: In 4738 the 7 sits in the hundreds place, so its value is 7 × 100 = 700. Expanded: 4000 + 700 + 30 + 8.

questions.prompt: Which is the GREATEST: 3999, 4100 or 4099?

options.diagnosis: Dazzled by the three 9s; thousands come first.
Compared the last digits (9 > 0) instead of working left to right.

options.text: They are equal — all have 4 digits
options.diagnosis: Same length does not mean same value; compare place by place.

questions.explanation: Thousands first: 4100 and 4099 both have 4 thousands, beating 3999. Then hundreds: 1 hundred beats 0 hundreds, so 4100 is greatest.

nodes.title: 3-digit Addition and Subtraction
nodes.description: Adding and subtracting 3-digit numbers uses the same regrouping ideas as 2-digit work — just with a hundreds column too. Carries can travel from ones to tens to hundreds, and borrowing can even cross a zero. Estimating first tells us roughly what to expect, so wild answers get caught.
learning_outcomes: Can add two 3-digit numbers with one or more carries
Can subtract 3-digit numbers with borrowing, including across a zero
Can estimate a sum or difference to the nearest hundred before computing
Can check subtraction by adding back
Can solve story problems needing 3-digit addition or subtraction

misconceptions.description: In each column the smaller digit is subtracted from the larger, whatever is on top — 500 − 243 gives 343.
misconceptions.signal: Never borrows; every column shows the positive difference of its two digits.
misconceptions.remedy: Estimate first (500 − 243 is about 250 — can 343 be right?). Then rebuild with base-ten blocks: to take 3 ones from 0 ones, a ten must be opened. Top number is the starting amount; order matters.

misconceptions.description: Borrowing across a zero goes wrong — the zero is skipped or never repaid (403 − 187 gives 316 or 296).
misconceptions.signal: Errors cluster exactly on problems with a 0 in the middle of the top number.
misconceptions.remedy: Rename before subtracting: 403 is 3 hundreds + 9 tens + 13 ones (open one hundred into tens, one ten into ones). Write the renamed number fully, THEN subtract column by column.

misconceptions.description: Numbers of different lengths are lined up from the left — 345 + 62 becomes 345 + 620.
misconceptions.signal: Answers are wildly large when adding a 3-digit and a 2-digit number.
misconceptions.remedy: Always align the ONES column (right edge), like books pushed to the right end of a shelf. Use squared paper with one digit per box and label the columns O, T, H.

real_world_hooks: Total runs across two innings of cricket
Money left from ₹500 after shopping
Kilometres between towns on a road sign
Books in the library before and after new ones arrive
teaching.video_search: 3 digit addition subtraction regrouping borrowing across zero grade 3

questions.prompt: What is 367 + 258?

options.diagnosis: Forgot to carry the ten from 7 + 8 = 15 into the tens column.
Forgot to carry the hundred from the tens column into the hundreds.
Subtracted instead of adding.

questions.explanation: Ones: 7 + 8 = 15 — write 5, carry 1. Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12 — write 2, carry 1. Hundreds: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Answer: 625.

questions.prompt: What is 500 − 243?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in every column.
Borrowed through the zeros but never reduced the 5 hundreds to 4.
Added instead of subtracting.

questions.explanation: Rename 500 as 4 hundreds + 9 tens + 10 ones. Ones: 10 − 3 = 7. Tens: 9 − 4 = 5. Hundreds: 4 − 2 = 2. Answer: 257. Check: 257 + 243 = 500. ✓

questions.prompt: A book fair had 725 books. 268 books were sold. How many books are left?

options.diagnosis: Borrowed for the tens but forgot to reduce the hundreds.
Added instead of subtracting — 'sold' means the pile shrinks.

questions.explanation: 725 − 268: ones 15 − 8 = 7; tens 11 − 6 = 5; hundreds 6 − 2 = 4. So 457 books are left. Estimate check: 700 − 270 ≈ 430 — close to 457, sensible.

nodes.title: Multiplication Tables and Facts (2–10)
nodes.description: The multiplication tables from 2 to 10 are the fact family of arithmetic — knowing them by heart makes every later calculation faster. But tables are more than a chant: each fact is an array you can picture, facts connect (7 × 6 is 7 × 5 and 7 more), and order never matters. Special rules for 0 and 1 complete the set.
learning_outcomes: Can recall multiplication facts for tables 2 to 10
Can use a known fact to derive a nearby one (7 × 6 = 7 × 5 + 7)
Can explain why n × 0 = 0 and n × 1 = n
Can use the turn-around rule: a × b = b × a
Can find the missing factor in facts like 6 × __ = 42

misconceptions.description: Multiplying by 0 or 1 works like adding — 6 × 0 = 6 and 6 × 1 = 7.
misconceptions.signal: Treats × 0 as 'changes nothing' and × 1 as 'add one'.
misconceptions.remedy: Tell group stories: 6 plates with 0 laddoos each — how many laddoos? None! 6 plates with 1 each — exactly 6. Contrast side by side with 6 + 0 and 6 + 1.

misconceptions.description: Table recall slips to a neighbouring fact — 7 × 8 becomes 48 or 54 (an answer from the row or column next door).
misconceptions.signal: Wrong answers are themselves multiples from adjacent facts (6 × 8, 6 × 9, 7 × 7).
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor and derive: from the secure fact 7 × 7 = 49, get 7 × 8 = 49 + 7 = 56. Use array cards where adding one more row is visible, and drill the few 'slippery' facts separately.
