misconceptions.description: a × b and b × a are separate facts that might differ — every table entry is memorised twice or recounted.
misconceptions.signal: Knows 8 × 7 instantly but freezes on 7 × 8; recounts from scratch after swapping.
misconceptions.remedy: Rotate one array card a quarter turn: the same dots show both facts. Then cross out duplicates on a full tables chart — nearly half the chart vanishes, a genuine relief!

real_world_hooks: 4 wheels per car in a parking lot
Runs from hitting sixes: 6, 12, 18...
Egg trays of 6 and idli plates of 4
Packets of 5 pencils — how many in 8 packets?
teaching.video_search: multiplication tables 2 to 10 tricks arrays derived facts grade 3

questions.prompt: What is 7 × 8?

options.diagnosis: Slipped to the nearby fact 6 × 9 = 54.
Slipped to the neighbouring fact 6 × 8 = 48.
Added 7 + 8 instead of multiplying.

questions.explanation: 7 × 8 = 56. If it slips your mind, derive it: 7 × 7 = 49, and one more 7 makes 56. (Rhyme: 5-6-7-8 → 56 = 7 × 8!)

questions.prompt: What is 9 × 0?

options.diagnosis: Treated × 0 like + 0, which changes nothing.
Wrote a zero after the 9 — that is multiplying by 10, not by 0.

questions.explanation: 9 × 0 means 9 groups with NOTHING in each — 0 + 0 + ... + 0 = 0. Any number times zero is zero.

questions.prompt: Rohan knows 4 × 6 = 24. Now he needs 6 × 4. What should he do?

options.text: Nothing new — it's the same total, 24; order doesn't matter in multiplication
Start skip counting from the beginning — the answer might be different

options.diagnosis: Thinks swapping the factors changes the total slightly.
Fell back to addition under uncertainty.

questions.explanation: A 4-row, 6-column array turned sideways becomes 6 rows of 4 — same dots, same total. So 6 × 4 = 4 × 6 = 24. Every fact you learn gives you its twin for free!

nodes.title: Multiplying 2-digit by 1-digit Numbers
nodes.description: To multiply a number like 47 by 3, we split it by place value: 3 × 40 and 3 × 7, then add the parts. Written short, this becomes the column method with carrying. BOTH parts of the number must be multiplied — that is the heart of the method.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number using expanded form (area model)
Can use the column method with carrying
Can estimate the product first (47 × 3 is about 50 × 3 = 150)
Can solve story problems involving equal groups of 2-digit amounts

misconceptions.description: Each digit is multiplied separately and the full partial answers are written side by side — 47 × 3 becomes 1221 (12 and 21).
misconceptions.signal: Products have far too many digits; both partial products appear glued together.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the area model: 47 × 3 = (40 × 3) + (7 × 3) = 120 + 21, then ADD the parts to get 141. The parts combine by addition, never by sitting next to each other.

misconceptions.description: The carried tens are written but never added — 47 × 3 gives 121 instead of 141.
misconceptions.signal: Answers are short by exactly the carry amount; the little carry digit sits unused above the column.
misconceptions.remedy: Slow the ritual: multiply, THEN add the carry, say it aloud: '3 × 4 = 12, plus 2 carried = 14'. Cross out each carry once used. Estimation (47 × 3 ≈ 150) flags the short answer.

misconceptions.description: Operations mix mid-problem — ones are multiplied but tens are added (23 × 3 → 3 × 3 = 9, 2 + 3 = 5, giving 59).
misconceptions.signal: The ones digit of the answer is right but the tens come from addition.
misconceptions.remedy: Label both partial products in the area model: 'this box is 3 × 20, this box is 3 × 3 — both are TIMES'. Have the student say the operation aloud for each column before computing.

real_world_hooks: Cost of 4 movie tickets at ₹35 each
24 students per class in 3 sections
Distance: 15 km each day for 6 days
Boxes of 12 bangles
teaching.video_search: multiply 2 digit by 1 digit area model column method grade 3

questions.prompt: What is 12 × 4?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied only the ones (2 × 4 = 8) and copied the tens digit unchanged.
Multiplied the ones but ADDED the tens digit to 4 (1 + 4 = 5).
Added 12 + 4 instead of multiplying.

questions.explanation: Split by place value: 12 × 4 = (10 × 4) + (2 × 4) = 40 + 8 = 48. Both parts of 12 get multiplied by 4.

questions.prompt: What is 47 × 3?

options.diagnosis: Forgot to add the carried 2 tens: 3 × 4 = 12, plus 2 makes 14.
Added 47 + 3 instead of multiplying.

questions.explanation: Ones: 7 × 3 = 21 — write 1, carry 2. Tens: 4 × 3 = 12, plus the carried 2 = 14. Answer: 141. Estimate check: about 50 × 3 = 150. ✓

questions.prompt: One bus ticket costs ₹35. How much do 4 tickets cost?

options.diagnosis: Dropped the carry: 5 × 4 = 20, the 2 tens never got added.
Wrote the partial products 12 and 20 side by side.
Added 35 + 4 instead of multiplying.

nodes.title: Division: Sharing, Grouping and Inverse of Multiplication
nodes.description: Division answers two kinds of questions: sharing (12 laddoos among 3 children — how many each?) and grouping (12 laddoos, 3 per bag — how many bags?). It is multiplication run backwards: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 because 3 × 4 = 12. Sometimes things don't share out evenly, and what's left over is the remainder.
learning_outcomes: Can solve sharing and grouping problems by acting them out or drawing
Can write and read division sentences (12 ÷ 3 = 4)
Can use a multiplication fact to solve a division (12 ÷ 3 via 3 × ? = 12)
Can handle simple leftovers (remainders) in sharing stories

misconceptions.description: Division is commutative like addition — 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 are the same thing.
misconceptions.signal: Swaps the numbers freely; reads any division as 'big number divided by small'.
misconceptions.remedy: Act out both stories: 12 laddoos among 3 children (4 each) versus 3 laddoos among 12 children (not even one each!). The order tells WHO gets shared to — it completely changes the story.

misconceptions.description: The answer to a sharing problem is the divisor itself — '12 shared among 3' is answered '3'.
misconceptions.signal: Echoes the second number as the answer; confuses 'how many groups' with 'how many in each'.
misconceptions.remedy: Always label the answer with its unit: '4 laddoos EACH'. Deal objects out one round at a time like playing cards, then count one child's pile.

misconceptions.description: Everything always shares out evenly — leftovers are ignored or silently discarded.
misconceptions.signal: Says 13 balloons among 4 friends gives '3 each' with no mention of the extra balloon.
misconceptions.remedy: Share real counters and put leftovers in a 'remainder dish' that must always be reported: '3 each AND 1 left over'. Discuss what could happen to the extra one.

real_world_hooks: Sharing laddoos or biscuits equally among friends
Dealing cards for a game
Making teams of 4 for kho-kho
Packing 30 rotis into boxes of 5
teaching.video_search: division as sharing and grouping remainder grade 3

questions.prompt: 12 laddoos are shared equally among 3 children. How many laddoos does each child get?

options.diagnosis: Echoed the number of children instead of finding each child's share.
Multiplied 12 × 3 instead of dividing.
Subtracted 12 − 3 instead of dividing.

questions.explanation: Deal them out: each child gets 1, then another, then another, then one more — 4 each. Check with multiplication: 3 × 4 = 12. ✓

questions.prompt: Is 12 ÷ 3 the same as 3 ÷ 12?

options.text: No — sharing 12 among 3 is a different story from sharing 3 among 12
Yes — order never matters in maths

options.diagnosis: Right answer, wrong reason: computed 12 ÷ 3 anyway, ignoring the order.

questions.explanation: 12 ÷ 3 = 4: three children get 4 laddoos each. But 3 ÷ 12 asks to share just 3 laddoos among 12 children — each gets only a small piece! Order matters in division.

questions.prompt: 13 balloons are shared equally among 4 friends. What happens?

options.text: Each gets 3 balloons, and 1 balloon is left over
Each gets 3 balloons, nothing is left
options.diagnosis: 3 × 4 = 12, but there were 13 — one balloon vanished!
Divided by 3 instead of 4 — swapped the numbers.

options.text: It cannot be shared at all
options.diagnosis: Thinks division stops working when the sharing isn't exact.

questions.explanation: 4 friends × 3 balloons = 12 balloons used, and 13 − 12 = 1 balloon remains. We say 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1. The leftover must always be reported!

nodes.title: Fractions: Half, Quarter, Third
nodes.description: A fraction names a fair share: a half is one of 2 EQUAL parts, a third is one of 3, a quarter is one of 4. The parts must be equal — a big piece and a small piece are not halves! Because quarters are smaller than halves, the more parts we cut, the smaller each part becomes.
learning_outcomes: Can fold or cut a shape into halves, thirds and quarters — with EQUAL parts
Can name and write 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 for one part of an equally divided whole
Can explain that 1/2 of the same whole is bigger than 1/4
Can find half or a quarter of a small collection (half of 8 mangoes)

misconceptions.description: Fraction parts need not be equal — ANY 2 pieces are 'halves', any 4 pieces are 'quarters'.
misconceptions.signal: Cuts a roti into one big and one small piece and calls both halves; accepts unequal shading of 1/4.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the fairness test: two hungry children must both be happy with EITHER piece — would they swap without fuss? Fold paper shapes and check parts match exactly by stacking.

misconceptions.description: A bigger denominator means a bigger piece — 1/4 must beat 1/2 because 4 beats 2.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses a quarter of a chocolate over a half 'because 4 is more than 2'.
misconceptions.remedy: Fold two same-size rotis (paper circles): one into halves, one into quarters. Lay 1/2 on top of 1/4 — seeing the half swallow the quarter beats any argument. More cuts = smaller pieces.

misconceptions.description: A fraction is two separate whole numbers — 1/2 is read as 'a 1 and a 2'.
misconceptions.signal: Reads 1/2 as 'one, two'; treats the top and bottom numbers as unrelated counts.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor language before symbols: say 'one out of 2 equal parts' every time while pointing at a real cut shape. Introduce the written form only after the spoken form is automatic.

real_world_hooks: Sharing a roti or paratha fairly
Half-time in a football match
Quarter plate at the canteen
Breaking a chocolate bar with a sibling — who checks fairness?
teaching.video_search: fractions half quarter third equal parts grade 3

questions.prompt: A roti is cut into 4 EQUAL parts. What is one part called?

options.diagnosis: Uses 'half' for any piece of anything — a half is one of exactly 2 equal parts.
Mixed up the number of parts; a third comes from 3 equal parts.
Answered with the count of parts instead of naming one part.

questions.explanation: Four equal parts means each part is one-fourth, also called a quarter, written 1/4 — one out of 4 equal parts.

questions.prompt: You may take 1/2 or 1/4 of the SAME chocolate bar. Which is more chocolate?

options.diagnosis: Both are 'one piece', but the pieces are different sizes.
Sees only unrelated whole numbers, not shares of the same bar.

questions.explanation: Cutting into 2 parts gives big pieces; cutting into 4 gives small ones. One of 2 equal parts (1/2) is more than one of 4 equal parts (1/4). More pieces means smaller pieces!

questions.prompt: Ria cuts her sandwich into 2 pieces — one big, one small. She says, 'Each piece is a half.' Is she right?

options.text: No — halves must be 2 EQUAL pieces
Yes — any piece of a sandwich is a half
No — a sandwich cannot be cut into halves
options.diagnosis: Over-corrected: it can, but only with equal pieces.

questions.explanation: Cutting into 2 pieces is not enough — halves must be equal. Try the fairness test: would both eaters happily take either piece? Only then are they true halves.

nodes.title: Money: Making Bills, Adding and Subtracting Amounts
nodes.description: Real shopping needs real arithmetic: adding up a bill with several items, multiplying when we buy more than one of something, and working out change from ₹50 or ₹100. Remember that 100 paise make ₹1, and always check: change must be less than what you handed over!
learning_outcomes: Can add amounts of money to make a simple bill
Can find the change from ₹50 or ₹100
Can multiply a price by a small quantity within a bill
Can convert between rupees and paise (₹1 = 100 paise)
Can judge whether a total or change is reasonable

misconceptions.description: Paise are treated as rupees — ₹5 and 75 paise becomes 'eighty rupees'.
misconceptions.signal: Adds the paise number straight into the rupee total; writes ₹5.75 as ₹80.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a two-column money mat (₹ | paise) with real or play coins. Exchange 100 loose paise for a ₹1 coin so the 100-to-1 relationship is physical, then re-add.

misconceptions.description: Change is found by adding the price and the payment.
misconceptions.signal: For a ₹34 toy paid with ₹50, announces ₹84 change — more than the note handed over!
misconceptions.remedy: Count up on a number line: 34 → 40 (6) → 50 (10 more) = ₹16 change. Install the sanity check as a rule: change must ALWAYS be smaller than what you gave.

misconceptions.description: In a bill, the quantity is ADDED to the price instead of multiplying — 2 notebooks at ₹25 costs ₹27.
misconceptions.signal: Bill lines show price + quantity; totals come out far too small.
misconceptions.remedy: Write bills with one row per item copy first: 25 + 25, then compress to 2 × 25 = 50. Estimate each line before computing: 'two twenty-fives must be about fifty'.

real_world_hooks: Making a kirana-shop bill for the week's groceries
Checking the canteen bill: 2 samosas and a juice
Saving up for a ₹250 cricket bat
Train tickets for the whole family
teaching.video_search: money word problems making bills change rupees paise grade 3

questions.prompt: Ria buys a toy for ₹48 and a ball for ₹35. How much does she spend in all?

options.diagnosis: Forgot to carry the ten from 8 + 5 = 13.
Wrote the 13 ones without regrouping into a ten.
Subtracted the prices instead of adding them.

questions.explanation: ₹48 + ₹35: ones 8 + 5 = 13 — write 3, carry 1. Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Total: ₹83.

questions.prompt: A kite costs ₹36. You pay with a ₹50 note. How much change should you get?

options.diagnosis: Borrowed for the ones but forgot to reduce the tens (5 − 3 instead of 4 − 3).
Slip while counting up from 36 to 50 — recount 36 → 40 is 4, then 10 more.

questions.explanation: Count up: 36 → 40 is ₹4, then 40 → 50 is ₹10; 4 + 10 = ₹14. Check: change (₹14) is less than the note (₹50). ✓

questions.prompt: Bill: 2 notebooks at ₹25 each, and 1 pen for ₹15. What is the total?

options.diagnosis: Added 25 + 2 + 15 — the quantity was added instead of multiplying.
Charged for only one notebook — forgot the quantity 2.
Charged for the notebooks three times (75) — one 25 too many.

nodes.title: Lines, Corners and Shape Composition
nodes.description: Shapes are built from lines and corners: straight lines, curved lines, sides that meet at corners. A shape keeps its name however it is turned — a tilted square is still a square. And shapes combine: two equal triangles can join to make a square, tangram pieces build pictures. Composing and decomposing shapes is geometry's version of adding and subtracting.
learning_outcomes: Can identify straight and curved lines in drawings and objects, in any direction
Can count sides and corners of polygons and use them to name shapes
Can recognise a shape in any orientation
Can compose new shapes from tangram-style pieces and predict what two shapes will make

misconceptions.description: Only horizontal (or 'level') strokes count as straight lines — a slanted edge is 'not a proper line'.
misconceptions.signal: Rejects slanted or vertical edges as straight lines; tilts head or paper to 'fix' them.
misconceptions.remedy: Test straightness with a taut string or ruler edge held against lines in EVERY direction. Rotate the page: the line stays straight however it leans — straight is about not bending, not about direction.

misconceptions.description: A shape's name changes with its orientation — the tilted square becomes a 'diamond', a sideways triangle isn't a triangle.
misconceptions.signal: Renames rotated cut-outs; says the shape 'changed' after turning.
misconceptions.remedy: Decide names by COUNTING, not by looking: 4 equal sides and 4 square corners is a square in any position. Rotate cut-outs slowly and recount together after each turn.

misconceptions.description: Shapes cannot combine into different shapes — two triangles can only ever make 'a bigger triangle'.
misconceptions.signal: Surprised when two triangles form a square; doesn't experiment with joining pieces different ways.
misconceptions.remedy: Free play with tangram or cut paper: challenge the child to make a square, a rectangle AND a big triangle from the same two pieces. Predict first, then test.

real_world_hooks: Tangram puzzles and paper folding
Kolam/rangoli made of straight and curved lines
Roof triangles and window rectangles on houses
Chapati (curve) vs samosa (straight edges)
teaching.video_search: lines corners sides shapes tangram composing shapes grade 3

questions.prompt: Which of these is a STRAIGHT line?

options.text: The slanted side of a ladder leaning on a wall
The rim of a round plate
options.diagnosis: The rim curves all the way round — it bends, so it is not straight.
Bent means not straight, even if parts of it look straight.

options.text: None — a slanting edge is not a straight line

questions.explanation: Straight means 'does not bend' — direction doesn't matter! A leaning ladder's side is perfectly straight even though it is slanted.

questions.prompt: Ria turns a square cut-out to stand on one corner. What shape is it now?

options.text: Still a square — 4 equal sides, 4 square corners
A diamond — it is not a square any more

options.diagnosis: Attended only to the pointed top corner, not the whole shape.

questions.explanation: Count, don't just look: it still has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners, so it is still a square. Turning a shape never changes what it is.

questions.prompt: Arjun has 2 equal triangles (a square cut along its diagonal). What can he make by joining them edge to edge?

options.text: A square, or a bigger triangle — depending on which edges he joins
Nothing new — triangles can't make other shapes

options.diagnosis: Straight-edged pieces can never make a curved shape.

questions.explanation: Join the two long edges: a square. Join two short edges: a bigger triangle. The same pieces make different shapes depending on how they meet — try it with paper!

nodes.title: Length in Centimetres and Metres; Estimation
nodes.description: Centimetres measure small things (your finger is about 1 cm wide) and metres measure big things (a big step is about 1 m). There are 100 centimetres in 1 metre. Reading a ruler from the 0 mark, choosing the right unit and estimating before measuring make us smart measurers.
learning_outcomes: Can measure lengths in cm with a ruler, starting from the 0 mark
Can state that 1 m = 100 cm and pick cm or m sensibly for an object
Can estimate lengths using body benchmarks before measuring
Can measure correctly even when the object doesn't start at 0 (broken-ruler problems)

misconceptions.description: A ruler is read at the finishing mark regardless of where the object starts — an object from 1 cm to 9 cm is '9 cm long'.
misconceptions.signal: Measurements are consistently off by one (or by wherever the object was placed); counts marks instead of the gaps between them.
misconceptions.remedy: Give deliberately 'broken ruler' tasks where 0 is missing: length = end mark − start mark, or count the SPACES between marks. Measure the same pencil from 0 and from 1 and reconcile the readings.

misconceptions.description: Units are decoration — 2 cm, 2 m and plain '2' all mean about the same.
misconceptions.signal: Says 'the door is 2 tall'; happily accepts that a door might be 2 cm high.
misconceptions.remedy: Build body benchmarks: fingernail ≈ 1 cm, giant step ≈ 1 m. Test silly claims against them: 'Could a door really be two FINGERNAILS tall?' Always say the unit with the number.

misconceptions.description: 1 metre converts to 10 centimetres (or whatever feels tidy) — the 100 relationship isn't secure.
misconceptions.signal: Converts m to cm by adding a zero sometimes, two zeros other times; says 2 m = 20 cm.
misconceptions.remedy: Unroll a metre tape and count the centimetre marks in tens: 10, 20, ..., 100. Lay ten 10-cm rods along a metre stick — exactly ten of them fit, making 100 cm.

real_world_hooks: Measuring your height on the wall chart
The tailor's metre tape
Long jump on sports day
How wide is your maths book in cm?
teaching.video_search: measuring length centimetres metres ruler estimation grade 3

questions.prompt: How many centimetres make 1 metre?

options.diagnosis: Mixed up with 1 km = 1000 m (or 1 kg = 1000 g).
Confused the metre with the 30 cm school ruler.

questions.explanation: 1 metre = 100 centimetres. Count along a metre tape in tens — 10, 20, 30 ... 100 — and you reach exactly one metre.

questions.prompt: A pencil lies along a ruler with one end at the 1 cm mark and the other end at the 9 cm mark. How long is the pencil?

options.diagnosis: Read only the finishing mark, ignoring that the pencil starts at 1.
Read the starting mark instead of the length.

options.text: You can't measure unless it starts at 0
options.diagnosis: Length is the distance BETWEEN the ends, wherever they sit.

questions.explanation: Length is the gap between the two ends: 9 − 1 = 8 cm. Starting at 0 is convenient, but any start works if you subtract.

questions.prompt: Which is the best estimate for the height of a door?

options.diagnosis: That is the width of a finger — the unit was ignored.
About the length of a pencil — far too short for a door; benchmark not used.
That is taller than a building! Estimate slipped by ten times.

questions.explanation: A tall adult is under 2 m, and doors are a little taller than people — about 2 m. Benchmarks (fingernail ≈ 1 cm, big step ≈ 1 m) make estimates sensible.

nodes.title: Weight (g, kg) and Capacity (mL, L)
nodes.description: We weigh things in grams and kilograms (1 kg = 1000 g) and measure liquids in millilitres and litres (1 L = 1000 mL). Choosing the right unit matters: a pencil in grams, a rice sack in kilograms; a spoon of medicine in mL, a bucket in litres. Balances and measuring jars turn 'heavier' and 'holds more' into exact numbers.
learning_outcomes: Can state 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 L = 1000 mL
Can choose sensible units (g/kg, mL/L) for everyday objects and containers
Can read simple weights and volumes from balances and measuring jars
Can compare and add simple weights and capacities in the same unit

misconceptions.description: The bigger or fuller-looking object is the heavier one; the taller container holds more.
misconceptions.signal: Judges parcels by size and bottles by height without weighing or pouring.
misconceptions.remedy: Keep surprising: weigh a big packet of chips against a small jar of pickle; pour a tall bottle into a short wide vessel. Prediction before every test.

misconceptions.description: The conversion is 100, not 1000 — 1 kg = 100 g, 1 L = 100 mL — or numbers are compared across different units directly.
misconceptions.signal: Converts with two zeros; says '500 is more than 1, so 500 mL beats 1 L'.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a kilogram from ten 100 g packets, counting 100, 200, ..., 1000. Fill a 1 L bottle with five 200 mL cups. Rule: convert to the SAME unit before comparing any two amounts.

misconceptions.description: Units belong to object types, not amounts — 'heavy things are kg things, light things are g things', so 1 kg of cotton weighs less than 1 kg of iron.
misconceptions.signal: Says a kilogram of iron beats a kilogram of cotton; refuses to weigh feathers in kg.
misconceptions.remedy: Put a weighed 1 kg cotton bundle and a 1 kg iron weight on the two pans of a balance — they level exactly. Same number + same unit = same weight, whatever the stuff.

real_world_hooks: Buying 1 kg tomatoes and 500 g chillies at the mandi
The milk packet: 500 mL
Water bottles for the school trip: 1 L each
The sabziwala's balance and iron weights
teaching.video_search: grams kilograms millilitres litres measuring weight capacity grade 3

questions.prompt: 1 kilogram = how many grams?

options.diagnosis: The kilo- step is a thousand, not ten.
That is HALF a kilogram — the weight of the small sugar packet.

questions.explanation: Kilo means one thousand: 1 kg = 1000 g. Ten packets of 100 g stack up to exactly one kilogram.

questions.prompt: Which is heavier: 1 kg of cotton or 1 kg of iron?

options.diagnosis: Judged by the material's reputation, not the measured amount.
The cotton bundle looks much bigger, but big is not heavy.
The whole point of units: 1 kg is 1 kg of anything.

questions.explanation: Both are 1 kg — the same weight! The cotton makes a huge fluffy bundle and the iron a small block, but a balance shows them perfectly level.

questions.prompt: A tall thin bottle holds 500 mL. A short wide jug holds 1 L. Which holds more?

options.text: The jug — 1 L is 1000 mL, more than 500 mL

options.diagnosis: Compared the numbers while ignoring the units.
Guessed equality without converting to the same unit.

questions.explanation: Convert to the same unit first: 1 L = 1000 mL. Now compare: 1000 mL > 500 mL, so the short wide jug holds more — height fools the eye!

nodes.title: Reading the Clock and Calendar
nodes.description: The clock's long hand counts minutes in fives — pointing at 3 means 15 minutes past. The short hour hand creeps between numbers: at half past 4 it sits halfway from 4 to 5, but the hour is still 4. Together with the calendar's dates, days and months, clocks let us plan and keep our promises on time.
learning_outcomes: Can read times to the half and quarter hour, and to 5 minutes
Can explain what each hand shows, including the hour hand between numbers
Can count minutes in fives around the clock face
Can find how many days between two dates on a calendar

misconceptions.description: The two hands are read the wrong way round — the long hand is taken for the hour.
misconceptions.signal: Reads half past 4 as 'about 6 o'clock' because the long hand points at 6.
misconceptions.remedy: Return briefly to a one-handed hour clock, then add the minute hand with a different colour. Sort hand jobs aloud before every read: 'short = hour, long = minutes'.

misconceptions.description: The minute hand's number is its face value — long hand on 6 means 6 minutes past.
misconceptions.signal: Says 4:06 for half past 4, 3:03 for quarter past 3.
misconceptions.remedy: Write the minute values (5, 10, 15...) in small numbers around a practice clock face and chant round in fives. Fade the small numbers once counting by 5s from 12 is automatic.

misconceptions.description: The hour hand between two numbers belongs to the LATER number — at 4:30 it is 'half past 5'.
misconceptions.signal: Hour read as 5 whenever the hand has left 4, even slightly.
misconceptions.remedy: Watch the hour hand travel across a whole hour (or turn the knob slowly): it leaves 4 at 4:00 and only ARRIVES at 5 at 5:00. Rule: the hour is the number the hand has PASSED, not the one it approaches.

real_world_hooks: School bell times and the class timetable
Train departure times at the station
TV cartoon show timings
Counting days to your birthday or Diwali on the calendar
teaching.video_search: telling time half past quarter past five minutes clock grade 3

questions.prompt: The LONG hand points to 6 and the SHORT hand is halfway between 4 and 5. What time is it?

options.diagnosis: Read the hour hand at the number it is approaching, not the one it passed.
Read the minute hand's 6 at face value; on 6 it means 30 minutes.
Took the long hand for the hour hand.

questions.explanation: Long hand on 6 = 30 minutes past. The short hand has passed 4 but not reached 5, so the hour is still 4. Time: half past 4 (4:30).

questions.prompt: The long (minute) hand points to 3. How many minutes past the hour is it?

options.diagnosis: Confused quarter past (on 3) with half past (on 6).
Counted round the wrong way — 45 is the 9, quarter TO the hour.

questions.explanation: Each number on the clock is worth 5 minutes for the long hand: 5, 10, 15. On the 3, it is 15 minutes past — quarter past the hour.

questions.prompt: Riya's exam is on 15 March. Today is 8 March. How many days are left until the exam?

options.diagnosis: Counted today as a waiting day as well as the 15th.
Added the two dates instead of finding the gap.
Stopped counting one day early — count 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15.

questions.explanation: Count from tomorrow to the exam day: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 — that's 7 days. Or subtract: 15 − 8 = 7.

nodes.title: Number Patterns: Skip Counting, Even and Odd
nodes.description: Numbers make patterns of their own: skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s from any starting point, and the even-odd rhythm that alternates forever. A number is even if it splits into pairs with none left over — and you can tell just by looking at its ones digit. Spotting these patterns builds the number sense that powers multiplication and algebra.
learning_outcomes: Can skip count by 2s, 5s and 10s starting from any number
Can say whether a number is even or odd using the ones digit
Can explain even numbers as 'splits into pairs with none left over'
Can describe and extend a number pattern by stating its rule

misconceptions.description: Even or odd is decided by the FIRST digit or by the number's size — 23 is 'even because 2 is even'.
misconceptions.signal: Judges parity from the tens/hundreds digit; big numbers are called even 'because they are big'.
misconceptions.remedy: Pair up 23 counters: one is always left alone — 23 is odd. Then link to the shortcut: only the ONES digit decides, because tens always split into pairs (10 = 5 pairs).

misconceptions.description: Zero in the ones place is neither even nor odd — 30 'ends in nothing'.
misconceptions.signal: Sorts 30, 40, 100 into a 'neither' pile; hesitates on any number ending in 0.
misconceptions.remedy: Pair up 30 counters — every counter finds a partner, none left over, so 30 is even. Extend the even endings list to 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and test it on round numbers.

misconceptions.description: Skip counting must start at the skip number itself — you can count 5, 10, 15 but a pattern like 3, 8, 13 is 'not allowed'.
misconceptions.signal: Refuses or fails to continue +5 patterns that don't start at 5; restarts them from 5.
misconceptions.remedy: Make equal jumps on a number line from different starting stones: +5 from 3 lands on 3, 8, 13, 18. The RULE is the jump size — the starting point is free.

real_world_hooks: House numbers: odd on one side of the street, even on the other
Counting money in ₹5 coins
Pairing shoes and socks
Skipping-rope counting games
teaching.video_search: skip counting even odd numbers pattern rules grade 3

questions.prompt: Skip count by 5s: 35, 40, 45, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Added 1 instead of the jump of 5.
Skipped a jump — 55 comes after 50.
Repeated the last term instead of jumping on.

questions.explanation: Each jump adds 5: 35, 40, 45, 50. Counting by 5s always lands on numbers ending in 5 or 0.

questions.prompt: Is 23 even or odd — and why?

options.text: Odd, because the ones digit 3 is odd — one counter is left without a pair
Even, because 2 is an even digit
Even, because 23 can be split into two parts
options.diagnosis: Any number splits into two parts; even needs two EQUAL parts with none left over.

options.text: Odd, because it is a smallish number
options.diagnosis: Size has nothing to do with even and odd.

questions.explanation: Pair up 23 objects: 11 pairs form and 1 is left alone, so 23 is odd. Shortcut: look only at the ones digit — 3 is odd, so 23 is odd.

questions.prompt: A pattern goes 3, 8, 13, 18, ... What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Added 1 instead of the pattern's jump of 5.
Jumped 6 — check each earlier jump: they are all exactly 5.

questions.explanation: Every jump is +5: 3 → 8 → 13 → 18 → 23. Skip counting can start anywhere — the rule is the jump, not the starting number.

nodes.title: Tables and Simple Bar Charts
nodes.description: A table lines data up in rows and columns; a bar chart turns those numbers into bars whose heights we can compare at a glance. To read a bar we follow its top across to the scale — and when one step of the scale stands for 2 or more, we must multiply, not just count steps. Charts help us answer questions with evidence.
learning_outcomes: Can record counts in a table using tally marks
Can read values from a simple bar chart using its scale
Can answer most/least and how-many-more questions from a chart
Can draw a bar chart from a small table of data

misconceptions.description: Bars are read by counting steps as ones, ignoring the scale — a 5-step bar on a 2-per-step scale is read as 5.
misconceptions.signal: All answers are exactly half (or a fixed fraction) of the true values on scaled charts.
misconceptions.remedy: Write the scale in a box at the top BEFORE reading anything, and count along the axis aloud: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Re-plot the same data at 1-per-step and 2-per-step and compare.

misconceptions.description: 'How many more?' is answered with the name of the bigger category, not a number — or with the bigger value itself.
misconceptions.signal: Q: 'How many more chose cricket than carrom?' A: 'Cricket!' (or '12').
misconceptions.remedy: Model difference as a climb: put a finger on the shorter bar's top and count up to the taller bar's top. The answer to 'how many more' is always a NUMBER of steps, not a name.

misconceptions.description: Questions about the data are answered from opinion or memory instead of the chart.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'football is most popular because everyone loves football' while the chart shows cricket.
misconceptions.remedy: Enforce point-to-prove: every answer needs a finger on the bar that shows it. Ask 'what does the CHART say?' and celebrate answers that go against personal favourites.

real_world_hooks: Class survey: how do you come to school?
Runs per over as a bar chart
Favourite ice-cream flavours at a party
Vehicles passing the school gate in 10 minutes
teaching.video_search: reading bar graphs with scale tally marks grade 3

questions.prompt: Favourite games of Class 3 — Cricket: 12, Kho-kho: 8, Carrom: 6, Football: 10. How many children chose kho-kho?

options.diagnosis: Read the biggest value instead of the row asked about.
Read the neighbouring row (carrom) — check labels carefully.
Added all the values instead of reading one row.

questions.explanation: Find the kho-kho row and read its number: 8 children chose kho-kho.

questions.prompt: In the same data (Cricket 12, Carrom 6), HOW MANY MORE children chose cricket than carrom?

options.diagnosis: Named the bigger category — but 'how many more' asks for a number.
Added the two values instead of finding the difference.
Compared cricket with kho-kho (12 − 8) instead of carrom.

questions.explanation: 'How many more' means find the difference: 12 − 6 = 6. Six more children chose cricket than carrom.

questions.prompt: In a bar chart, each step on the scale stands for 2 children. The 'tea' bar is 5 steps tall. How many children does it show?

options.diagnosis: Counted the steps but ignored the 2-per-step scale.
Added the scale to the steps (5 + 2) instead of multiplying.
Miscounted 6 steps before doubling — recount the steps.

questions.explanation: Each step is worth 2, so 5 steps show 5 × 2 = 10 children. Always read the scale before reading the bars!
